title: Continued attacks between Pakistan and Afghanistan increase protection risks, food security needs, and access constraints in Afghanistan’s border provinces
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Humanitarian needs, particularly related to protection, food security, and access, are increasing and are at high risk of deteriorating further along the Durand Line between Afghanistan and Pakistan given the conflict escalation and air strikes between the two countries. Hostilities have spiked since 28 June 2026 along Aghanistan’s border provinces, including Kunar, Paktia, and Paktika, when a Pakistani attack killed 28 civilians and wounded 49. Pakistani authorities stated that the strikes targeted the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which they held responsible for a deadly militant attack in Karachi that killed three security personnel. Pakistan has consistently accused Afghanistan of harbouring armed groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians, including the TTP, which Islamabad accuses of operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan has denied these allegations and threatened retaliation against Pakistan for the air strikes.
The latest attack comes as part of a series of tit-for-tat attacks between Afghanistan and Pakistan that started in February. After launching Operation Ghazab lil Haq on 21 February, Pakistani authorities declared open war against Afghanistan's Interim Taliban Authority. Despite a two-week ceasefire beginning on 8 April negotiated by China, these attacks have continued, forming a pattern of ‘coercive diplomacy’ between the two countries. This coercive diplomacy has seen fighting continue until it becomes less productive for either side, at which point they briefly return to negotiations until a new security incident restarts the cycle. This pattern is expected to persist in waves over the next three to six months rather than resolve into a stable ceasefire.
The current tension heightens protection risks for civilians in border-adjacent Afghan provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika), including casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, as well as exposure to explosive remnants of war and unexploded ordnance in areas affected by shelling.
Displacement towards other regions of Afghanistan is expected to persist over the next three to six months. The closure of and restricted movement at the Torkham, Chaman, and other crossings along the Durand Line, whether from active conflict or checkpoint closures, could trap civilians in insecure areas or block access to services on the other side. Host communities already sheltering IDPs and returnees face added strain, raising the risk of tension and disputes over limited resources and services.
The closure of border crossings has also halted transit flows and delayed humanitarian and commercial supplies. Afghanistan is highly dependent on food imports, as domestic production cannot meet national demand. This dependence, combined with the depletion of harvest stocks in September and declining agricultural labour opportunities from the seasonal downturn in October, is likely to worsen food insecurity. As a result, market dependence is expected to increase, reducing household income and heightening the risk of food consumption gaps.
expectedImpact:
Populations along the Durand Line will experience high protection risks. Civilian casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, particularly in border-adjacent provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, and Paktika), will likely occur. There is also a high risk of damage to civilian infrastructure, homes, markets, and health facilities, reducing safe access to essential services.
An estimated 21.9 million people are in need across Afghanistan in 2026, including 15 million in need of protection and 4.2 million in need of shelter and site management support. This figure may not account for the estimated 500,000 conflict-displaced people.
The conflict is likely to impede access to services, deteriorate the livelihoods of people, particularly returnees recently reported from Pakistan and Iran. There were over 2.5 million returnees from Iran and Pakistan in 2025, adding pressure on overstretched local resources, services, and livelihoods.
Forced displacement is expected to persist and is likely to increase, causing a deterioration of humanitarian needs in provinces along the Durand Line. In April 2026 alone, over 9,000 families were forced to leave their homes given the rocket attacks conducted by Pakistani forces on areas near the Durand Line in Afghanistan’s Kunar province.
The provinces of Kunar, Laghman, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika are projected to remain in Stressed (IPC Phase 2) food security conditions or deteriorate to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) during the lean season. Paktika has been among the most affected provinces, experiencing repeated cross-border shelling that has damaged civilian infrastructure and displaced communities, reducing access to health services and agricultural livelihoods. The situation is partly caused by the prolonged closure of key Durand Line crossings, impeding the trade and import of food and directly affecting food security and livelihoods in Afghanistan. Growing uncertainty around commodity movements through Iran because of the volatile Middle East conflict is also driving up logistics costs and reducing the availability of essential goods in local markets. Further conflict escalation along the Durand Line is likely to  delay any reopening of border crossings and halt the limited humanitarian convoys currently permitted through, further reducing the availability of essential goods and deepening food insecurity.
The direct impact of conflict escalation on civilian protection and humanitarian access is expected to be the primary driver of increased need. Casualties, displacement, and restricted humanitarian access caused by persistent air strikes and border closures are likely to push additional populations into IPC 3 before food insecurity peaks. Up to 2.3 million additional people could become food-insecure as a result of a prolonged border closure with Pakistan and further conflict escalation. At the same time, food assistance currently reaches only 2.7% of the population because of governmental restrictions and funding shortfalls.
By October 2026, the depletion of household harvest stocks and the seasonal decline in agricultural labour will increase market dependence just as conflict-driven border closures at Torkham are expected to drive prices upwards through the lean season peak from December–January. The situation is compounded by high unemployment and declining remittance inflows.

updates.text: Protection risks for communities in border areas increased in September as clashes and cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan resumed after a temporary decline. Repeated Pakistani airstrikes and Afghan military operations have heightened the risk of civilian casualties, damage to homes, and displacement, particularly in eastern Afghanistan. Pakistan said its strikes on 21 September killed 28 fighters, while Afghan officials reported civilian casualties; the UN confirmed three civilian deaths. On 27 September, Afghan forces reported killing 28 fighters and capturing 32 in Nuristan province after they crossed from Pakistan. Further Pakistani strikes on 1 October targeted locations in Afghanistan, including Kunar and Helmand provinces. Pakistan reported 22 militants killed and weapons depots destroyed, while Taliban authorities reported 9–10 civilian deaths, including women and children, and damage to homes. The conflicting accounts highlight the risks to civilians in affected areas, where renewed hostilities could cause further casualties, displacement, and disrupted access to essential services.

triggers.title: Lethal militant attack in a major Pakistani urban centre.
triggers.description: A confirmed TTP attack targeting Pakistani security forces or government installations in cities such as Karachi, Peshawar, or Islamabad is likely to trigger further Pakistani airstrikes or ground operations in Afghan border provinces. Historically, such events have served as the primary political trigger for Pakistani retaliatory airstrikes and ground operations in Afghan border provinces like Paktia and Paktika. The 28 June attack was carried out by Pakistan, according to Pakistani authorities, in retaliation for an alleged TTP attack on security personnel in Karachi days earlier.

triggers.title: Cross-border hostilities
triggers.description: Clashes between army forces in bordering areas and the closure of borders will limit movement, constrain access of humanitarian aid, interrupt livelihoods and trade between communities. In past border closures food security and livelihoods have been significantly impacted.

title: Escalating clashes between Interim Taliban Authority forces and armed opposition groups in Badakhshan deteriorates food security and increases protection risks
riskType: New emerging risk
rationale:
Persistent tension in Badakhshan, driven by disputes over mining resources, ethnic differences, contested territorial control, and grievances over Interim Taliban Authority (ITA) governance, risk creating recurrent instability and protection risks for communities.
Armed opposition to the ITA has been building in the province over the course of 2026. ACLED recorded 22 anti-ITA armed-opposition events in Badakhshan between January–July 2026, up from just four between June–December 2025. While the recent surrender of Fateh-aligned fighters has eased the immediate risk of renewed clashes, the ITA's broader efforts to consolidate control over powerful opposition commanders and curb their influence are likely to generate resentment among these groups, increasing the risk of further infighting.
ACLED forecasts at least 34 violent events nationwide in September 2026, of which 19 (roughly 56%) are projected to occur in Badakhshan alone, meaning a 17% rise in violence against civilians compared to the previous month's average. This indicates Badakhshan province is becoming a potential point for national conflict risk.
The province has valuable mineral deposits, including gold and lapis lazuli, and has long been contested. Recent clashes were triggered by the ITA suspension of gold mining activities in parts of the province to disarm fighters of opposition groups.
Clashes have occurred across multiple districts in 2026, including a brief seizure of the Yaftal-e Sufla district headquarters and Afghanistan Freedom Front clashes with ITA forces in Zebak in July. Repeated fighting over district centres risks triggering intermittent displacement as families flee active front lines and may expose residents to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and casualties. Badakhshan’s current context indicates a risk of rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating food security outlook.
expectedImpact:
Intensified conflict would directly affect communities' protection, with people likely exposed to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and the risk of casualties. Repeated fighting over district centres could trigger short- and medium-term displacement as families flee active front lines, restricting mobility and disrupting livelihoods in turn.
Gold mining disputes between armed groups have disrupted local livelihoods. The ITA has suspended mining in contested areas to cut off income for opposition armed groups, in the process also stripping income from mining-dependent communities, which are not necessarily tied to armed groups. Badakhshan's mines department head reported around 650–700 mining companies, with thousands of people working manually. Thousands of miners are specifically deployed in areas such as Shiwa. Further escalation could mean lost income for miners caught between Taliban control efforts and dissident commanders. Health access, already limited, would likely deteriorate further; communities have already reported shortages of medicines and adequate facilities, as well as substance use in place of unavailable medicines. Escalating conflict increases the risk of health facilities being damaged, occupied, or forced to suspend services and could disrupt the already-limited supply of medicines to clinics.
This livelihood pressure is set against a difficult seasonal outlook. Above-average precipitation expected between October 2026 and April 2027 could damage the upcoming harvest, further eroding food security just as the lean season approaches. Food prices are already rising, and further disruption to markets, movement, and livelihoods could push households towards potentially harmful coping strategies, such as early marriage and skipping meals.
The current context in Badakhshan points to a compounding risk: rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating health and food security outlook.

updates.text: Clashes between armed groups and Taliban forces continued in Badakhshan province in September. Between 29 August and 25 September, battles increased by 68% (eight events) and organised violence by 31% (11 events) compared with the previous year’s average. On 30 September, the Afghanistan Freedom Front reported Taliban attacks in Zebak district, following repeated clashes in recent weeks. On 29 September, the Taliban Defence Ministry declared its operation over in Kamdesh district, Nuristan province, claiming 41 people killed and 62 detained. Continued fighting could expose rural communities to casualties, movement restrictions, forced recruitment, and disruptions to education and livelihoods, although these impacts remain unverified. Humanitarian needs are compounded by food insecurity: an estimated 671,800 people (at least 40% of Badakhshan’s population) face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse. Below-average harvests and above-national-average prices for rice, sugar, and cooking oil are likely to further constrain food access. Limited vaccination coverage and access barriers in remote areas also increase vulnerability to measles outbreaks.

title: Escalating cross-border insecurity linked to the Sudan conflict increases protection risks and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Since early 2026, the conflict in Sudan has evolved from a humanitarian crisis affecting Chad into a direct security threat to eastern border areas. Repeated drone strikes, cross-border incursions, and clashes involving fighters aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have already caused casualties on Chadian territory, including around Tine and other border regions. These incidents indicate a growing risk that the Sudan conflict could generate sustained military confrontations, proxy violence, or retaliatory attacks inside Chad. This risk is increasingly characterised by the possibility of sustained military confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces operating along the Chad–Sudan border.

This risk is driven by a convergence of security, economic, and political factors. The Chad–Sudan border has become a strategic corridor for the movement of fuel, arms, gold, and military supplies supporting groups involved in the Sudan conflict. Competition over these routes has transformed border areas into contested spaces where violence increasingly follows smuggling and supply networks. Recent attacks suggest a shift from incidental spillover to deliberate projection of force into Chadian territory.

The conflict is also aggravating existing vulnerabilities in Chad. Fractures within cross-border Zaghawa community networks, which remain influential within Chad’s security apparatus, have deepened as communities react to violence in Darfur and perceptions of Chad’s involvement in the conflict. Continued violence in Darfur, combined with Chad’s historical role in Sudanese proxy conflicts, increases the risk of elite defections, armed realignments, and renewed cross-border mobilisation. Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may also re-emerge, including support to armed groups and militias operating across the border, increasing the likelihood of retaliatory attacks and further regional destabilisation.

Over the next one to three months, further RSF incursions, SAF-backed proxy activity, or competition over border corridors could increase cross-border violence, displacement, protection risks, and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad. Additional attacks or retaliations would likely worsen conditions in provinces already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnees, further straining regional services, humanitarian operations, and community relations. The risk is not limited to humanitarian spillover and increasingly involves the possibility of sustained confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces.
expectedImpact:
Further escalation of cross-border violence linked to the Sudan conflict could expose eastern Chad to new levels of civilian casualties, trauma, and insecurity. Additional drone strikes, shelling, armed incursions, or proxy attacks in border areas such as Adré, Tine, and the surrounding areas may directly affect civilians, trigger new displacement, and increase protection risks in communities already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnees. Repeated exposure to violence and insecurity is also likely to increase psychological distress and trauma among affected populations.

Escalating military activity could damage or disrupt critical infrastructure, including transport routes, border facilities, health centres, markets, telecommunications infrastructure, and humanitarian supply corridors. Further insecurity along the Chad–Sudan border may reduce civilian mobility, restrict trade, and hinder humanitarian operations. If border crossings tighten or close, people fleeing violence in Darfur will find it more difficult to reach safety, and the delivery of humanitarian assistance and essential goods into eastern Chad will be limited.

Deteriorating security conditions may also increase public health risks. Displacement, overcrowding, disrupted health services, and reduced humanitarian access could contribute to disease outbreaks and weaken regional health systems’ response capacity. If violence expands or becomes sustained, humanitarian needs are likely to increase significantly across eastern Chad, particularly in border areas already facing limited service availability and weak coping capacities.

updates.text: The risk remains active, although no significant new cross-border attacks inside Chad were identified during the second half of September. Humanitarian pressure linked to the Sudan conflict has nevertheless increased sharply as fighting in Darfur and other parts of Sudan drives renewed displacement across the border. By 25 September, more than 400 Sudanese refugees were crossing into Chad each day, around 20 times the rate recorded in previous months, bringing arrivals since the beginning of 2026 to more than 55,000. The acceleration in arrivals is increasing pressure on already overstretched reception areas and services in eastern Chad, while funding constraints affect humanitarian organisations' capacity to provide shelter, food, and relocation assistance. Continued conflict in neighbouring Sudan therefore maintains the risk of further refugee arrivals and humanitarian deterioration in eastern Chad, while the potential for renewed cross-border security incidents remains, given the heightened military presence and tensions established along the border following the August strikes.

The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as cross-border violence increasingly affected Chadian territory and prompted stronger security measures. On 21 August, Chad accused Sudanese Armed Forces aircraft and drones of striking a convoy more than 100km inside Ennedi-Est province, prompting authorities to raise the regional alert level to its highest and deploy additional forces. On 28 August, an air strike near the border killed at least 12 people at a fuel market, further increasing civilian protection risks and concerns over escalation.

The risk remains active after slightly deteriorating in July. Cross-border insecurity continues along eastern Chad, with new drone attacks reported on 21 July near Tiné amid intensified hostilities in Darfur. One strike in Indour hit a water point, causing livestock losses and possible human casualties, while another damaged an administrative vehicle in Bamina. Between 17 June and 17 July, 23 security incidents were recorded, killing 23 people, nearly half concentrated in Ouaddai and Wadi Fira. Chadian authorities have continued disarmament operations and movement controls in Sila, reflecting persistent concerns over cross-border armed activity. Humanitarian pressures have also increased. Despite the official border closure, 4,126 new refugees arrived in July, while protection conditions during displacement worsened. The proportion of households reporting at least one human rights violation during flight increased from 53% in June to 58% in July, with reported physical violence rising from 22% to 29%. More than 220,000 refugees remain stranded in insecure border areas awaiting relocation, increasing their exposure to insecurity and limited access to services. Over the coming months, further drone strikes, cross-border violence, or proxy mobilisation could further restrict safe movement across eastern Chad and increase protection risks for refugees, returnees, and host communities. The continued backlog of relocations, rainy season access constraints, and the potential suspension of WFP food assistance from September would likely amplify the humanitarian consequences of any further deterioration in border security.

The risk remains active and has slightly deteriorated. Recent reporting indicates that border insecurity continues to affect eastern Chad, with refugee arrivals from Sudan slowing in May likely because of insecurity around crossing points, including a 26 May drone strike in Al-Tina. This supports the risk logic that violence linked to the Sudan conflict is increasingly affecting Chadian border areas and limiting safe mobility rather than only generating humanitarian spillover. The humanitarian exposure remains high. As of 21 June, 932,771 Sudanese refugees had arrived in Chad since April 2023, while 400,914 Chadian returnees were also recorded. Most new arrivals remain concentrated in Ouaddaï, Wadi Fira, Sila, and Ennedi Est, including 234,499 in Wadi Fira and 509,637 in Ouaddaï. UNHCR also reports that 87% of registered people are women and children and 13% have specific needs.
Protection risks are also increasing. Border monitoring between 1–15 June found that 63% of interviewed households fled Sudan because of insecurity, 42% reported human rights violations during flight, and 49% had family members still blocked in Sudan, mainly because of lack of transport means. In Wadi Fira, continued Zaghawa–Tama tensions and clashes have restricted movement and access to essential SRH and GBV services. UNFPA also reports a 90% funding gap, severely limiting life-saving SRH and protection services.
Over the next one to three months, further drone strikes, cross-border violence, or proxy mobilisation could further restrict movement across the Chad–Sudan border, increase protection risks, and strain humanitarian operations in eastern Chad. The acceleration of refugee relocations from unstable border areas to safer inland sites shows that insecurity remains a direct operational concern. If insecurity persists, humanitarian actors may face greater access constraints while refugees, returnees, and host communities face worsening protection, health, and service-access risks.

triggers.description: Additional drone strikes, shelling, or armed incursions near the Chad–Sudan border, particularly around Adré, Tina, and other eastern border localities, increase civilian casualties, trigger further displacement into Chad, and constrain humanitarian operations in already fragile border areas. Continued insecurity may also disrupt cross-border trade and movement routes relied upon by refugees and host communities
triggers.objective: 100% completion would be reached if cross-border attacks become sustained and recurrent, affecting multiple border localities in eastern Chad and causing significant civilian casualties, displacement, or humanitarian access disruptions.

triggers.title: Attacks on strategic infrastructure in Chad
triggers.description: Threats by Sudanese actors against Chadian airports, border facilities, military positions, or transport infrastructure may materialise into direct attacks on strategic assets in eastern Chad. Any strike against airports such as Amdjarass, military installations, or critical transport corridors would increase the risk of direct confrontation between Chad and Sudanese armed actors, disrupt humanitarian and commercial operations, and further destabilise border regions
triggers.objective: 100% completion would be reached if attacks directly target strategic infrastructure in Chad, including airports, military facilities, border posts, or major transport corridors, causing significant disruption to civilian, humanitarian, or commercial activities.

triggers.title: Renewed proxy mobilisation and cross-border armed group activity
triggers.description: Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may re-emerge through the mobilisation, arming, or support of rebel groups and allied militias operating along the border. Increased involvement of SAF-aligned groups, RSF-linked actors, Darfuri armed factions, or Chadian rebel networks could expand the conflict beyond isolated border incidents and increase the likelihood of retaliatory attacks on Chadian territory.

title: Escalating insecurity across the Lake Chad Basin increases displacement, protection risks, and humanitarian access constraints
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Violence involving Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) is rising after five years of declining lethality in the Lake Chad Basin. More than 300 clashes involving the two groups were recorded in the first quarter of 2026, 30% above the previous quarter, while militant Islamist-linked fatalities increased by 28% over the past year, reaching their highest level since 2015. Nigeria accounted for 87% of these fatalities, with Borno remaining the expected epicentre, followed by affected areas of Adamawa and Yobe.
The escalation is expected to be driven by two related developments. While regional forces have concentrated military operations against ISWAP, Boko Haram has regrouped and rebuilt its capacity to launch coordinated attacks against military bases. At the same time, the May killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal Al Minuki is expected to trigger retaliatory attacks and greater competition between factions for territorial influence and legitimacy. ISWAP has overrun at least 16 Nigerian military bases over the past year, while its increasing use of improvised explosive devices and reconnaissance drones enhances its capacity to identify, isolate, and attack military positions, increasing the operational threat posed by the group.
Over the next three to six months, there is a very high probability that intensified insurgent attacks and military counteroperations will increase civilian casualties, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints across the basin. Violence is expected to remain concentrated in Borno, with continued spillover into Adamawa and Yobe, where Boko Haram and ISWAP are likely to intensify attacks on civilians, military positions, and transport routes. Escalating violence in northeastern Nigeria is expected to generate additional refugee movements into Niger's Diffa region, while military pressure and cross-border armed group movements may contribute to increased attacks, abductions, and disruptions to fishing and trade in Cameroon’s Far North, as well as renewed displacement and protection risks in Chad’s Lac province. These cross-border displacement dynamics and parallel insecurity are expected to reverse recent stabilisation gains and generate additional humanitarian needs across the Lake Chad Basin.
expectedImpact: Borno state is expected to remain the epicentre of the crisis, with intensified attacks by ISWAP and Boko Haram likely to generate additional displacement, civilian casualties, and humanitarian access restrictions. Spillover into Adamawa and Yobe may further disrupt transport corridors, markets, and access to health and education services in affected communities. In Niger’s Diffa region, the main humanitarian impact is expected to result from additional refugee arrivals fleeing violence in northeastern Nigeria, increasing pressure on host communities, protection services, and humanitarian assistance. In Cameroon’s Far North, renewed attacks, abductions, and restrictions on fishing and cross-border trade may further erode livelihoods and increase protection risks in border communities. In Chad’s Lac province, renewed attacks and military operations may trigger secondary displacement, restrict civilian movement, and increase pressure on already-overstretched basic services. Across the basin, increased insecurity is expected to further constrain humanitarian access, particularly along transport routes and in remote border and island communities. Additional displacement and livelihood disruptions are likely to increase humanitarian needs and place further pressure on civic authorities and humanitarian responders across the four countries.

updates.text: The risk continued to increase in the second half of September, with persistent armed group activity generating new displacement and protection concerns in Cameroon's Far North region. On 17 September, armed assailants killed at least 15 civilians in Madegoua, near Makary commune in Logone et Chari division. While no group claimed responsibility, a security analyst assessed that Islamic State West Africa Province was likely responsible. The attack prompted several hundred people from around ten nearby villages to flee towards Kousseri, Mora, and Waza, where new arrivals faced inadequate food and shelter and increased pressure on local health services. Insecurity remained persistent elsewhere in Far North region during September, including attempted attacks by Islamic State West Africa Province on security positions near Fotokol and continued Boko Haram abductions. These developments reinforce the risk of further displacement and protection needs in border communities and demonstrate that sustained armed group activity is translating into humanitarian impacts despite continued military operations.

The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as sustained Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province activity across the Lake Chad Basin continued to challenge security forces and disrupt civilian movement. In Borno, repeated attacks and insurgent logistics activity prompted intensified military operations, while 204 conflict-related incidents and 108 deaths were recorded in Cameroon’s Far North between 1 July and 25 August. Continued insecurity across border areas is increasing protection risks and constraining livelihoods and humanitarian access, reversing fragile stabilisation gains.

triggers.title: Retaliatory violence following the killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal al-Minuki
triggers.description: The reported killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal al-Minuki by US and Nigerian forces on 15 May 2026 could trigger retaliatory attacks by ISWAP, while intensifying competition with JAS/Boko Haram for territorial influence and operational relevance. Escalating attacks against military positions, civilians, and strategic infrastructure—particularly in Borno State—could increase displacement and humanitarian needs, while military pressure and cross-border armed group movements may generate spillover effects into Niger’s Diffa region, Cameroon’s Far North, and Chad’s Lac Province.
triggers.objective: Increased retaliatory attacks by ISWAP and/or JAS/Boko Haram following the killing of Abu-Bilal al-Minuki, resulting in sustained increases in attacks against military positions and civilians in Borno with spillover into neighbouring countries.

triggers.title: Expansion of military counteroffensives and emergency security measures
triggers.description: Nigerian and regional security forces may intensify military operations, including cross-border operations and emergency security measures, in response to rising insurgent activity. Expanded military deployments, movement restrictions, and operations around Lake Chad and border areas could increase civilian displacement, disrupt livelihoods, and further constrain humanitarian access, particularly if armed groups respond with additional attacks or shift operations across borders
triggers.objective: Expansion of Nigerian and regional military operations, including cross-border operations and movement restrictions, leading to increased civilian displacement and humanitarian access constraints across the Lake Chad Basin.

title: Peace talk end and military offensive against armed groups in Colombia escalate conflict and increase civilian casualties and displacement
riskType: New emerging risk
rationale:
After the elections in June 2026, Abelardo de la Espriella’s win as Colombia's new President signalled a major change in the country's stance towards non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and drug trafficking organisations. The President-elect has since announced an end to peace negotiations and a nationwide military offensive to begin once he takes office on 7 August, including a 90-day security crackdown involving military deployments, aerial operations, and coca eradication measures.
This shift may increase the risk of clashes, civilian casualties, displacement, and confinement, particularly in Pacific Coast departments, including Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca, as well as in Norte de Santander and Putumayo, which were among Colombia’s most conflict-affected areas in 2025.
This risk is compounded by the significant strengthening of NSAGs in recent years. Armed group membership has grown substantially since 2022. Armed groups have simultaneously expanded into new territories, adopted new warfare tactics, including the use of explosive drones, and extended social control against communities, including curfews and checkpoints. Ahead of the anticipated offensive, NSAGs are expected to intensify operations to consolidate territorial control, while retaliatory actions during the crackdown could further increase civilian harm. In response, the elected President has proposed Plan Colombia 2.0, aimed at recovering NSAG-controlled territory, eradicating coca cultivation and illegal mining (the primary financing sources for armed groups), and securing record investment in state armed forces, with the political and financial support of the US Government.
As a result, July, the month preceding the new Government's inauguration, is expected to see an intensification of NSAG violence as armed groups seek to consolidate territorial control and prepare ahead of the anticipated military offensive. Over the first 90-day period (August–October), a marked increase in armed clashes with state forces is expected, a trend that should persist throughout the remainder of 2026. These dynamics will directly affect civilian populations in the departments highlighted, where most rural and Indigenous communities reside.
Planned government reforms, including major cuts to state bureaucracy and measures targeting officials linked to the previous administration, could also increase political tensions and trigger social mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the risk.
A historic ‘Super El Niño’ event, forecast to intensify through late 2026, is expected to compound these dynamics. Authorities are warning of extreme heat, drought, and water shortages, with national implications for food security. This adds further pressure on communities in the departments covered by this risk, where access to food is already constrained by confinement and mobility restrictions linked to armed group activity.
expectedImpact:
The expected impact of intensifying NSAG activity and a state military offensive extends to the entire population of the departments highlighted, approximately 10.6 million people, who face risks of forced displacement, confinement, and attacks against civilians. Military operations and armed group retaliation are also expected to increase risks of civilian casualties, attacks against communities, and humanitarian access restrictions in affected areas. Illegal armed group membership has nationally grown by an estimated 23% over the past two years, reaching approximately 27,000 fighters by early 2026 – meaning any return to more active confrontation is likely to be more widespread than in recent cycles of violence.
As an illustrative precedent, the January 2025 escalation between the National Liberation Army (ELN) and dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia in Catatumbo (Norte de Santander) – one of the six departments covered by this risk – displaced an estimated 50,000–56,500 people within weeks of the breakdown of peace talks, underscoring how quickly displacement can scale once dialogue ends and active confrontation begins. This is included as 2025 historical baseline context rather than current reporting.
Armed groups in the region have intensified the recruitment of children, including through social media and by targeting rural boarding schools, while threatening teachers and relatives who report such cases. Nationally, child recruitment cases rose sharply through 2025. An intensification of these practices may be anticipated as groups seek to replenish ranks ahead of renewed confrontation.
Confinement – which already prevented over 137,000 people across the country from leaving their communities between January–August 2025, a significant increase from 2024 – is expected to further increase, restricting affected populations’ access to food, healthcare, and other essential goods and services. These impacts may be compounded by forecasted climate pressures, including drought and water shortages linked to the ‘Super El Niño’, which could further worsen food insecurity in communities already affected by conflict-related mobility restrictions.
Among the highlighted population, cross-border migrants and refugees living along the Venezuelan border who work in Colombia and periodically return home represent a high-risk group, as escalating conflict would hinder their international movement and their ability to afford food and housing. Farmers and Indigenous communities in the rural areas with the strongest NSAG presence are similarly disproportionately exposed.

updates.text: In September, intensified state operations and continued armed group activity sustained conflict-related protection risks in Colombia. Between January–August, 23,931 people were affected by mass displacement and 80,369 by confinement, with Cauca, Chocó, Norte de Santander, and Putumayo among the most affected departments. In August alone, 5,976 people were displaced and 6,201 confined. The Government’s shift towards military pressure has increased the lethality of operations against armed groups, while attacks using explosive drones remain a concern, particularly in Cauca and Norte de Santander. Further military pressure may redirect armed group activity towards state forces in the short term, while territorial competition, retaliatory attacks, and incursions into contested areas could sustain violence over the following months. Civilians in rural and Indigenous communities remain exposed to displacement, confinement, movement restrictions, and disrupted access to markets and livelihoods.

The risk deteriorated during August 2026 as the new Government’s military offensive coincided with intensified armed group violence and growing civilian exposure. In Sipí and Nóvita municipalities, Chocó department, fighting between the Clan del Golfo and National Liberation Army (ELN) since 10 August has restricted mobility and livelihoods, displaced hundreds of families, and confined other communities; a 23 August drone attack injured three civilians and displaced 90 families to Barranco, Charco Hondo, and Charco Largo. The Government conducted air strikes against the ELN in Tibú and San Calixto municipalities, Norte de Santander, on 10 August and against dissident groups of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia in El Retorno and Miraflores municipalities, Guaviare, on 27 and 30 August. The first two operations killed at least four minors. In El Patía municipality, Cauca, suspected Carlos Patiño members attacked security forces, while five improvised explosive devices were found on the Pan-American Highway. These events indicate that the anticipated escalation is materialising through simultaneous non-state armed group violence, intensified state operations, and increased risks to civilians and key transport routes.

Since the election of right-wing politician Abelardo de la Espriella as President of Colombia, the activities of non-state armed groups (NSAGs) in Colombia's peripheral departments have increased especially in July 2026, intensifying the likelihood of rising humanitarian impacts. In Norte de Santander, a department in eastern Colombia on the border with Venezuela, the NSAG known as the National Liberation Army (ELN) attacked with explosive-laden drones the main airport in Catatumbo subregion; in the department of Chocó, west of the country, the ELN kidnapped 39 people while they were travelling along a main departmental road. Other NSAGs also stole armoured vehicles, set up illegal checkpoints, and engaged in combat against the armed forces in departments such as Cauca and Valle del Cauca, south of Chocó in western Colombia. In response, the new de la Espriella Government has announced an offensive against illicit crops and illegal mining, the main source of financing for NSAGs, as well as an operation to reassert state control over territories in the departments of Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Norte de Santander, where these groups are the strongest.

triggers.title: Launch of the 90-Day Security Crackdown
triggers.description: The incoming government’s planned military offensive against NSAGs from 7 August, including bombing campaigns against armed group camps, aerial coca fumigation, deployment of Joint Task Forces to Cauca, Chocó, and Nariño, and increased defence investment, is expected to provoke armed group retaliation against security forces and civilians perceived to be cooperating with the State.

triggers.title: NSAG consolidation and territorial expansion
triggers.description: The significant strengthening of NSAGs since 2022, including a reported increase in membership, territorial expansion, adoption of new tactics, and increased reliance on illicit economies such as coca cultivation and illegal mining, increases the likelihood that armed groups will seek to consolidate control over contested territories and demonstrate operational capacity ahead of and during the anticipated offensive.

triggers.title: Formal termination of peace negotiations
triggers.description: A decision by the incoming government to end the outgoing administration’s “Total Peace” talks with NSAGs would remove an important mechanism for dialogue and de-escalation. The breakdown of ELN talks preceding the escalation of fighting in Catatumbo (Norte de Santander) in January 2025 illustrates how quickly violence and displacement can increase following the collapse of negotiations.

triggers.title: Bureaucratic cuts and public sector purges
triggers.description: Implementation of the pledged 40% reduction in the state apparatus and removal of officials linked to the outgoing administration could trigger sustained protest mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the security risk through potential clashes with security forces and increased protection concerns.

title: Forecast below-average Kiremt rains in Ethiopia threaten food production and livelihoods
riskType: New emerging risk
rationale:
El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration puts the probability of El Niño from May–July at around 61%, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre's May 2026 forecast indicates a high likelihood of below-normal June–September Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia, with above-normal temperatures. Severe localised deficits are likely in the northeast and central areas, with at least 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more.
Kiremt is the primary rainy season for Ethiopia's northern and central cropping areas, governing the Meher harvest – the country's most important crop season, which produces the most teff, maize, sorghum, wheat, and barley across Amhara, Central Ethiopia, Oromia, the Southern regions, and Tigray. Below-average rainfall would cut yields and household food production. In Tigray and Amhara, poor rains may also reduce agricultural labour income during the June–August lean season.
In past El Niño episodes, Meher maize and sorghum production fell across Ethiopia, most sharply in eastern Amhara,  northeastern Oromia, and Tigray; national yields dropped by around 2% below normal, with localised deficits of 10–15%. High fertiliser and fuel prices will likely limit farmers' input use during planting, lowering yield potential even with adequate rainfall, while raising transport costs for inputs and produce.
Staple food prices are already exceptionally high; annual food inflation reached 13.5% in April, up from 11% in March but down from 15.6% in April 2025 – a renewed monthly acceleration after disinflation, not a sustained year-on-year worsening. Drivers include increased fuel costs from Middle East conflict-linked energy disruptions, seasonal lean season food supply tightening, and trade disruptions, which are severely straining poor rural households.
El Niño typically also boosts the October–December rainfall across lowland/riverine eastern East Africa. Forecasts show a very high chance of above-average rainfall across central and eastern Ethiopia, likely driving flooding in flood-prone lowlands.
expectedImpact:
Below-average Kiremt rainfall would directly reduce Meher crop yields across Ethiopia's northern and central highlands, where teff, maize, sorghum, wheat, and barley are the primary staples. Reduced production would tighten household food stocks ahead of the post-harvest period, drive staple prices higher in already severely stressed markets, and eliminate the seasonal agricultural labour opportunities that poor rural households depend on for income during the lean season. In the pastoral south and southeast, accelerated pasture and water scarcity from June onwards would drive livestock migration, increase mortality rates, and further suppress milk availability – deepening food insecurity in areas where IPC 3 is already widespread and herd recovery from successive droughts remains incomplete. A poor Kiremt season would likely push significant numbers of households currently in IPC 3 into IPC 4, with the most exposed areas being the northeastern and central highlands, where rainfall deficits are forecast to be most severe, and the eastern pastoral zones of Somali region.
Should El Niño enhance the October–December rains as forecast precedent suggests, flood-prone lowland areas of Ethiopia face a contrasting but equally damaging set of impacts. Flooding would damage infrastructure, displace communities, and disrupt market supply chains at a time when households are already weakened by a poor Kiremt season.
Across both hazards, limited data availability, elevated humanitarian funding gaps, and access challenges in parts of the country severely constrain the response capacity. If both the Kiremt drought and October–December flooding materialise, Ethiopia faces a sustained and deepening deterioration in humanitarian conditions through the end of 2026 and into early 2027.

updates.text: The risk remained stable in September, with conditions continuing to follow the drought-then-flood pattern expected under El Niño. Rainfall deficits during the June–September Kiremt rains exceeded 50% of average across much of the country, and the Meher harvest, which provides over 85% of national crop production, could be up to 30% below average, with the worst-affected areas being Tigray, eastern Amhara, Afar, and eastern Oromia regions. Slight late-season improvements in rainfall are unlikely to help earlier planted crops substantially, although later planted crops may benefit. In northeastern pastoral areas, deficits have rapidly depleted surface water and increased distances to watering points, while pasture in the southeast is deteriorating after the rains ended. Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected to persist through January 2027 across many drought-affected areas, with some households facing Emergency (IPC Phase 4). October–December rainfall is forecast to be above average, with up to a 90% probability of enhanced rainfall in southern Ethiopia. In September, the Ethiopian Meteorological Institute warned of flash flooding and landslides in southwestern, southern, and southeastern lowlands, with rainfall up to 75% above normal in parts of the south. The institute also cautioned that unseasonal rains in northern, northeastern, and eastern areas could damage mature crops ready for harvest, meaning drought and flood impacts could occur at the same time in different parts of the country.

The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as parts of central and northern Ethiopia experienced a very poor start to the June–September Kiremt season, with persistent rainfall deficits accompanied by soil-moisture and vegetation stress. These conditions have increased concerns over reduced agricultural production and productivity, as well as pressure on pasture and water resources. El Niño is forecast to strengthen through late 2026.

triggers.title: Developing El Niño conditions forecast to suppress June–September Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia's key Meher-producing areas
triggers.description: Climate forecasts indicate a high and rising likelihood of El Niño conditions developing by 2026, strengthening through the second half of the year. ICPAC's May 2026 forecast points to a high probability of below-normal Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia, with precipitation deficits likely in the northeastern and central areas, where there is at least a 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more. This combination of reduced rainfall and above average temperatures during the critical Kiremt season is expected to suppress Meher crop yields, reduce agricultural labour demand, and accelerate pasture and water scarcity in pastoral areas.

triggers.title: Strengthening El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December season in lowland and riverine areas of Ethiopia
triggers.description: El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during the October–December season across eastern East Africa. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, there is an increased likelihood of flooding across flood-prone lowland areas of Ethiopia, especially the Somali Region. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa.

title: Intensifying forest and peatland fires across Indonesia cause prolonged hazardous haze, health impacts, and education, transport, and livelihood disruptions
riskType: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
rationale:
Indonesia's annual forest and peatland fire season has intensified sharply during the 2026 dry season. Nearly 95,000 hectares burnt in July alone, almost doubling the area burnt during the first six months of the year and bringing the January–July total to more than 202,000 hectares. By late August, around 285,000 hectares had burnt, and thousands of hotspots were being detected across Kalimantan and Sumatra. West Kalimantan, including Ketapang and Pontianak, is among the areas most affected, while fires are also concentrated in Central Kalimantan and parts of Sumatra, particularly Jambi, Riau, and South Sumatra.
The risk could deteriorate over the next one to three months as El Niño conditions intensify and prolong hotter, drier weather. Fire risk normally peaks during the late dry season, while peatland fires can burn underground, spread beyond visible fire lines, and remain difficult to extinguish. Agricultural land clearing and fires within company concessions are also contributing to the ignition and spread. More than 9,000 hotspots were recorded in August, exceeding the number recorded in the same month during the severe 2015 fire season.
Haze is already affecting populated areas across Kalimantan and Sumatra, particularly Jambi city, Palangka Raya in Central Kalimantan, Pekanbaru in Riau, and Pontianak and Singkawang in West Kalimantan, where poor air quality and reduced visibility have disrupted education and transport.
Indonesia has substantial national response capacity. The National Agency for Disaster Countermeasure, provincial authorities, the military, police, and forestry services are conducting ground suppression, water bombing, cloud seeding, hotspot surveillance, and law enforcement operations. By the end of August, authorities had mobilised around 48,000 officers, more than 1,400 volunteers, and 34 firefighting aircraft, while permits had been issued for foreign aircraft. Even so, persistent peat fires, limited water, poor visibility, and simultaneous fires across remote areas could exceed local response capacity and prolong exposure to hazardous smoke. Humanitarian organisations may be required to provide targeted health, education, and livelihood support if the haze persists or national capacity becomes overstretched.
expectedImpact:
If the risk materialises, prolonged hazardous haze would primarily affect health, education, transport, and livelihoods across fire-prone areas of Kalimantan and Sumatra.
Repeated exposure to PM2.5 and other pollutants could increase acute respiratory infections, asthma attacks, eye and skin irritation, and cardiovascular complications. Children, older people, pregnant women, outdoor workers, and people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions would face the greatest risk. Persistent hazardous air quality could increase outpatient consultations and hospital admissions and place additional pressure on provincial health services, particularly in remote areas where healthcare access is already limited.
Additional school closures or restrictions on outdoor activity could interrupt learning for children in affected provinces. Dense smoke and reduced visibility could delay or cancel flights, disrupt road and river transport, and constrain access to health facilities, markets, and remote communities. Fire damage and prolonged haze could also reduce household income by interrupting farming, fishing, construction, transport, and plantation work. Localised crop, livestock, or household food stock losses are possible near active fires, but a national or regional food supply crisis is not currently expected.
Indonesia is likely to retain overall leadership of the response. Humanitarian organisations may be required to support respiratory disease surveillance and treatment, the distribution of effective masks, clean-air assistance, risk communication, education continuity, and targeted support to remote, low-income, and Indigenous communities if hazardous conditions persist or local capacity is overwhelmed.

updates.text: The risk increased during September, with haze continuing to disrupt education and transport despite a decline in fire activity. By 9 September, more than 250,000 pupils across 1,030 schools in Palembang, South Sumatra, had shifted to remote learning, while around 12,800 schools were closed across Sumatra and Borneo. Over 1.4 million students were learning online across affected areas of Indonesia. Since 11 September, haze has reduced visibility in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, to below 1km, disrupting flights for several days and hampering firefighting operations. Although high-confidence fire hotspots declined significantly in Central and West Kalimantan by 14 September, and none were recorded in Riau, fires continued in parts of Kalimantan. Smoke transported from other provinces has also sustained haze in affected areas. Continued fires and cross-provincial smoke are likely to prolong exposure to hazardous air pollution, disrupt transport and education, and constrain firefighting efforts.

triggers.title: Sustained increase in hotspots and peatland fires
triggers.description: A continued rise in hotspots and burned area across West and Central Kalimantan, South Sumatra, Riau, and Jambi, particularly where fires spread into deep peat, would indicate that suppression operations are not containing the fire season. Fires persisting underground or reigniting after initial suppression would increase the likelihood of prolonged smoke exposure.

triggers.title: Prolonged dry conditions and peak El Nino
triggers.description: Below-average rainfall, extreme heat, declining water availability ahead of El Nino peak towards the end of 2026 could dry vegetation and peat further. This would allow fires to spread more rapidly and simultaneously across several provinces, stretching firefighting capacity.

title: Forecast El Niño conditions threaten crop production and worsen food insecurity in Kenya
riskType: New emerging risk
rationale:
El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a 61% probability of El Niño from May–July, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts below-normal June–September (JJAS) rainfall across western and northern Kenya alongside above-normal temperatures nationwide, closely resembling the 2023 El Niño, when below-normal JJAS rainfall affected western Kenya.
The forecast threatens Kenya's principal food-producing areas during a critical stage of the long rains season. Over 70% of the country's annual crop production depends on the long rains, which extend into August–September in the North Rift and western Kenya. These areas had already recorded below-average rainfall in April and early May despite favourable national rainfall totals. Combined with delayed fertiliser deliveries, below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures from June–September are likely to reduce yields of maize, beans, sorghum, and sweet potato, resulting in a below-average October–November harvest.
In northern and eastern pastoral areas, above-average temperatures during the June–September dry season are expected to accelerate the deterioration of rangeland and water resources. Recovery remains fragile after the 2020–2023 drought and the 2023–2024 floods, with depleted herd sizes, persistent livestock disease, and reduced vaccination programmes limiting resilience.
The deteriorating production outlook comes as maize and bean prices remain 6–21% and 8–17% above the five-year average, respectively, driven by depleted household stocks following the poor 2025 short rains, high transport costs, and strong market demand. High household debt further constrains purchasing power. A below-average harvest would tighten domestic food supplies, drive prices higher, and further reduce incomes and food access for farming and pastoral households.
expectedImpact:
Below-average JJAS precipitation and above-average temperatures would directly threaten the October–November harvest of maize, beans, sorghum, and sweet potato across the North Rift and western Kenya – crops that represent the primary source of domestic food production. Reduced yields would tighten household food stocks at a time when they are already depleted, drive staple prices higher in already-stressed markets, and erode incomes for farming households with limited capacity to cope. In pastoral areas, accelerated rangeland deterioration and reduced water availability from June onwards would increase livestock mortality and reduce milk output, deepening food insecurity across the ASALs. IPC 3 outcomes, already widespread, are likely to expand in geographic scope and severity, with Emergency (IPC Phase 4) a credible risk in the most exposed pastoral counties. Acute malnutrition among children and pregnant and lactating women – already above emergency thresholds in refugee camps – is likely to worsen across both pastoral and camp populations as food access declines.
Should El Niño enhance the October–December short rains as forecast precedent suggests, eastern and coastal Kenya face a contrasting but equally damaging set of impacts. Flooding would damage standing crops, destroy infrastructure, and disrupt market supply chains at a critical point in the post-harvest period. Displacement from flood-affected areas would increase pressure on host communities and services already under strain. During the October 2023 to January 2024 El Niño short rains, at least 178 people died, and thousands of households were displaced.
Across both hazards, the response capacity will be constrained. Humanitarian funding gaps, reduced food ration levels, and limited government reach into remote pastoral and flood-affected areas mean that rising needs are unlikely to be fully met. If both the JJAS drought and October–December flooding materialise, Kenya faces a sustained deterioration in humanitarian conditions through the end of 2026 and into early 2027.

updates.text: El Niño has driven a dry spell that has cut Kenya's harvest and is now expected to bring above-average short rains and flooding, with Lamu county projected to reach Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Dadaab camp Emergency (IPC Phase 4) between October–January. The dry spell caused a poor long rains harvest, with maize production estimated at 22–28% below the five-year average and losses of up to 43% anticipated in high potential North Rift counties including Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu, and Nakuru. The Ministry of Agriculture has acknowledged widespread crop failure in the North Rift, which produces over 60% of Kenya's maize. Wholesale maize prices in Nairobi are expected to remain 9–19% above the five-year average until January 2027, limiting food access for poor households. The October–December rains are expected to improve pastoral conditions, but in Dadaab flooding is likely to last for weeks, limiting humanitarian access and increasing waterborne disease. IPC 3 outcomes are expected to persist in Garissa, Mandera, Tana River, Wajir, and Turkana counties through January, where flooding is likely to damage transport infrastructure and displace households. A national assessment has identified 18 counties and 5,660 health facilities in areas at risk of flooding.

triggers.title: Developing El Niño conditions forecast to suppress June–September rainfall across western and northern Kenya
triggers.description: Climate forecasts indicate a high and rising likelihood of El Niño conditions developing during May–July 2026, strengthening through the second half of the year. ICPAC's May 2026 forecast points to a high probability of below-normal JJAS rainfall across western and northern Kenya — where the unimodal long rains season in fact extends into August/September and has already tracked below average in April and early May — alongside above-normal temperatures. This combination is expected to reduce soil moisture during the critical grain-filling and maturation stages of long rains crops in the North Rift and western Kenya, directly threatening the October–November harvest. Pastoral areas across the ASALs are likely to experience accelerated rangeland deterioration and reduced water availability, compounding already fragile livestock recovery.

triggers.title: El Niño raises risk of flooding during the October–December short rains season in eastern and coastal Kenya
triggers.description: El Niño conditions are historically associated with enhanced rainfall during Kenya's October–December short rains season, particularly across eastern and coastal areas. During the 2023 El Niño, wetter-than-normal OND conditions across eastern Kenya materialised as severe and damaging flooding. With seasonal forecast anticipating high probability of above-average precipitation between October and December 2026, a comparable pattern of enhanced short rains is likely. This risk may also be compounded by the positive condition of the Indian Ocean Dipole, expected to start from August-September, which typically enhances the effects of El Nino in eastern Africa. Should this materialise, flooding would damage infrastructure and cropland in areas already weakened by successive climate shocks, further compounding humanitarian needs heading into early 2027.

title: El Niño drives drought conditions, increasing food insecurity and heightening humanitarian needs in Madagascar in 2027
riskType: New emerging risk
rationale: Current models indicate a very high probability for El Niño to develop by July 2026 and persist into early 2027. In Madagascar, El Niño typically drives precipitation and temperature anomalies, with dry conditions in southern parts of the country and heavy rainfall in the north and east. In 2015–2016 and 2023–2024, El Niño caused prolonged drought conditions and crop failure, resulting in increased food insecurity that particularly affected the country's south. Seasonal forecasts anticipate near-average precipitation in July–September and below-average precipitation across most of the country in October–December. The same forecasts indicate a very high probability of above-average temperatures across the entire country in July–December. Drier and hotter-than-average conditions may affect the start of the rainy season, which runs October–April and is essential for producing Madagascar's main staple cereals, such as maize and rice, harvested in April–June. This may lead to below-average yields, with severe consequences for the population's access to food in 2027, widening food consumption gaps and increasing malnutrition rates. Impacts may also extend to other staple crops, such as cassava, beans, and sweet potatoes, as well as to agricultural labour availability, which usually peaks between November–March. Limited rainfall and abnormally high temperatures may also reduce pasture availability, resulting in deteriorating livestock body conditions and increased morbidity and mortality. Dry conditions are also likely to affect access to water for domestic consumption, potentially leading to reliance on unsafe water sources and limiting hygiene and sanitation practices. These combined effects are expected to increase humanitarian needs, strain local coping mechanisms, and heighten dependence on external assistance, particularly among rural households already vulnerable to climate variability. The country shows a high pre-existing vulnerability to climatic shocks, including reliance on rainfed agriculture, limited water and sanitation infrastructure, and low coping capacity.
expectedImpact: The effects of El Niño-induced drought are expected to result in deteriorating food security, increased malnutrition, and heightened humanitarian needs. In the south, rainfall deficits are likely to lead to the most severe impacts, as the region already experiences prolonged dry conditions and a poor 2025–2026 rainy season. Across the country, similarly poor conditions in 2026–2027 may lead to reduced agricultural production, depletion of household food stocks, and increased reliance on markets, where purchasing power remains constrained because of poverty and limited income opportunities. This is expected to widen food consumption gaps, particularly among rural households dependent on rainfed agriculture. El Niño is also expected to significantly affect WASH conditions and public health. In southern areas, water scarcity will likely reduce access to safe drinking water and hygiene services. This is critical given that only about 36% of the rural population has access to improved water sources, and only around 10% use basic sanitation facilities, leaving many communities highly exposed to water shortages and unsafe practices. In contrast, above-average rainfall and cyclones in the north and east during El Niño periods can lead to flooding, contaminating water sources and increasing the spread of waterborne and vector-borne diseases such as cholera and malaria. Poor WASH access already contributes significantly to child mortality and illness. Across affected areas, pre-existing vulnerabilities such as high poverty, limited coping capacity, and weak infrastructure are likely to amplify the impact of these shocks. Malnutrition risks are expected to increase, particularly among children under five, driven by reduced food availability and access and deteriorated access to water, sanitation, and hygiene. At the same time, repeated shocks are likely to further erode households' coping strategies, pushing them to adopt coping mechanisms with potentially harmful consequences, including reducing food intake and selling productive assets.

updates.text: The risk has further increased in September 2026 as forecasts indicate a strong to very strong El Niño from October 2026 to February 2027, with below-average rainfall expected across parts of southern Madagascar (Androy, Anosy, and Atsimo-Andrefana regions) during the October–November start of the rainy season. Assessments indicate that the lean season has already started earlier than usual in the Grand South, with poor households exhausting food stocks in September following below-average 2025/26 harvests and increasingly relying on markets and negative coping strategies. Conditions are expected to deteriorate further from October, with around 3.7 million people (11% of the analysed population) projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between October 2026 and February 2027, including nearly 426,000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). El Niño-related rainfall deficits could further reduce 2027 crop production and household incomes, particularly in the Grand South, increasing food insecurity and humanitarian needs through early 2027, though past El Niño events had limited effects on national paddy output.

The risk has deteriorated since July 2026 as confidence in a strong El Niño event has increased, and forecasts continue to indicate elevated drought risks across southern Madagascar through late 2026 and early 2027. El Niño is projected to strengthen further and persist into early 2027, increasing the likelihood of below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures during the critical agricultural season. Recent food security assessments indicate worsening conditions in Grand Sud starting in October, with below-normal harvests, reduced household food stocks, and expectations of an early and more severe lean season. The number of people facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food insecurity is likely to increase between late 2026 and early 2027.

triggers.title: Rainfall deficits and above average precipitation affecting agricultural production
triggers.description: Dry conditions are likely to lead to reduced soil moisture, crop failure, and declining pasture availability, which in turn limit household food production and income from agriculture. This reduces food availability at the household level and increases reliance on markets at a time of constrained purchasing power.

title: Continued coordinated JNIM–FLA attacks and blockades increase protection risks, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints in Mali
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Since late April 2026, the unprecedented operational coordination between Jama’at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de libération de l’Azawad (FLA) has significantly increased pressure on Mali’s security apparatus and exposed vulnerabilities in state control across northern, central, and western regions. Over the next one to three months, three converging escalation dynamics will likely worsen humanitarian conditions significantly across Mali. The assassination of Defence Minister Gen. Sadio Camara on 25 April 2026 created a command vacuum in Mali's security apparatus leadership. As the junta’s chief military strategist and the primary architect of the partnership with Russia’s Africa Corps, his death is likely to severely hamper coordination of counter-offensive operations, make Malian-Russian tactical responses less cohesive, and embolden further advances by armed groups at a critical juncture of territorial contestation.

JNIM and the FLA are both targeting urban supply chains, favouring economic attrition strategies over military objectives. With the FLA explicitly signalling southward expansion following the capture of Kidal region, citing Gao and Tombouctou as its next targets, and JNIM threatening a full blockade of Bamako region along the Senegalese and Ivorian corridors, populations in major urban centres face mounting risks of acute fuel and food shortages. Critically low stocks in the capital mean any sustained suspension of truck traffic could rapidly disrupt electricity, healthcare, and water access for millions already living under severe humanitarian stress. Towns such as Bandiagara and Douentza are already becoming more isolated because of road insecurity and flight suspensions, significantly constraining humanitarian access and the movement of goods and people.

Escalating resource scarcity and growing disillusionment within the military following the Kidal withdrawal increase the likelihood of intra-junta fracture or countercoup in the coming weeks. Political instability at the centre would further constrain the junta's capacity to manage insurgent pressure, negotiate humanitarian access, and sustain basic service delivery, deepening civilian vulnerability across northern, central, and western Mali.
expectedImpact:
Continued conflict escalation is expected to significantly worsen humanitarian conditions across Mali over the next one to three months, compounding pre-existing vulnerabilities among an estimated 5.1 million people already needing assistance. Mali already hosts more than 414,000 IDPs, and the number is likely to surge as fighting intensifies in Gao and Tombouctou regions and spreads southward into Sikasso and Kayes regions. The conflict also threatens displacement of farming communities during the critical harvest season, which would amplify nationwide food insecurity risks. Mali's capacity to host refugees – including over 165,000 from Burkina Faso and Niger – will be further strained, placing additional pressure on already overstretched basic services in affected areas.

Attacks on transport corridors and supply routes may further disrupt fuel imports, commercial traffic, and market functionality, contributing to higher transportation and food prices and affecting the availability of essential goods and services. Continued insecurity along the Bamako–Kayes, Bamako–Ségou, and Bamako–Sikasso corridors could further affect the movement of fuel, food, and commercial goods into major urban centres. Additional pressure on electricity production and fuel supply systems could worsen existing disruptions to healthcare, water access, and telecommunications. Fuel shortages are already affecting ambulance referrals, emergency obstetric care, medical supply chains, and fuel-dependent health services in conflict-affected areas, particularly in northern and central Mali. If supply disruptions persist, urban populations in Bamako and secondary cities may experience prolonged electricity cuts, rising living costs, and reduced access to basic services.

Humanitarian responders are already facing significant operational constraints. Humanitarian flights have been repeatedly suspended, and WFP temporarily halted activities following the April attacks. Insecurity has made several destinations, including Ansongo, Douentza, Kidal, Niafunké, and Ménaka, partially or fully inaccessible. If attacks, blockades, and insecurity along key corridors persist, humanitarian access is likely to deteriorate further, delaying the delivery of assistance and reducing the reach of life-saving services.

Should political instability escalate into intra-junta fracture or a counter-coup, the collapse of security command structures would likely suspend humanitarian flights and road convoys entirely, cutting life-saving assistance to already inaccessible populations across northern and central Mali.

updates.text: The risk continued to increase during the second half of September as JNIM sustained high-intensity operations in central Mali, further challenging state control and security along strategic corridors. Following its 10 September attack on the Dioura military camp, which killed more than 100 soldiers and resulted in more than 100 being captured, JNIM shelled the Sévaré air base for six consecutive nights between 14–19 September and attacked a forward operating base in Konna on 20 September. The attacks indicate JNIM's continued capacity to target major military positions and transport corridors in Mopti region, while supply routes to Bamako remain exposed to disruption by armed groups. Although no significant new joint operation by JNIM and the Azawad Liberation Front was identified after the previous update, the sustained pressure by JNIM, alongside the continued presence and coordination capacity of both groups in northern Mali, maintains the risk of further territorial and humanitarian deterioration. Continued insecurity is likely to constrain population movement, trade, and humanitarian access, particularly across central and northern Mali.

The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as continued operations of Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin and the Azawad Liberation Front sustained pressure on state control in northern and central Mali. Fighting around Kidal contributed to the displacement of nearly 40,000 people, including around 15,000 who sought refuge in Gao and Ménaka regions, increasing pressure on already-strained services. Conflict involving non-state armed groups continued to disrupt markets, livelihoods, and supply routes, worsening food insecurity. From June–August, 1.56 million people faced Crisis (CH Phase 3) or worse food insecurity, including nearly 57,000 in Emergency (Phase 4).

The risk deteriorated further in July 2026. Although Malian and African Corps forces regained Anéfis following the fighting of 4–9 July, subsequent attacks show that they have not secured the surrounding territory or key transit routes.
