Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de libération de l'Azawad (FLA) continued joint operations against military positions and convoys in northern Mali, while JNIM intensified pressure in central Mali, including by taking the Kouakourou military camp and forcing the locality’s approximately 5,000 residents to flee. These developments confirm that the JNIM–FLA operational cooperation remains active and that armed groups retain the capacity to isolate strategic locations, disrupt military resupply, and generate new displacement. Humanitarian conditions have worsened alongside the escalation. More than half of Kidal’s population has moved towards Gao, Ménaka, or Algeria, while markets are operating at reduced capacity, and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food insecurity is expected to persist in Kidal and Ménaka. Attacks on civilians and vehicles continue to disrupt trade and movement elsewhere, while blockaded communities, such as Diafarabé, remain at risk of renewed shortages despite limited food deliveries. Humanitarian operations remain suspended in Kidal, and insecurity continues to restrict access in Gao, Mopti, and Tombouctou. Over the next one to three months, continued JNIM–FLA operations, insecurity along strategic corridors, and retaliatory military strikes are likely to generate further displacement and civilian protection risks while constraining trade and humanitarian assistance. Limited funding and access will further reduce the capacity to respond as food needs increase during the lean season.

The risk has deteriorated further. Since 4 July 2026, Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin and the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) have launched a new wave of coordinated attacks across northern and central Mali, including Aguelhok, Anéfis, Gao, and Sévaré. Armed groups have seized Anéfis town and continue to besiege the military camp, while clashes, shelling, drone attacks, aerial strikes, and attempts to reinforce the camp continue. The attack on a military convoy travelling from Gao towards Anéfis on 9 July indicates that the armed groups are sustaining pressure on strategic routes and military positions in Kidal region. The escalation confirms that coordinated JNIM–FLA operations remain active and are likely to further disrupt movement along key routes linking Gao, Kidal, and other northern areas. This increases risks of civilian exposure to armed violence, movement restrictions, new displacement, and humanitarian access constraints in areas already facing severe needs. Around 683,000 people live in the affected towns and surrounding regions, including approximately 363,000 already in need of humanitarian assistance. The deterioration comes amid persistent blockade-related impacts. Tombouctou has faced severe fuel shortages, disrupting electricity and water services, while there are reports of serious abuses by all conflict parties since the April escalation, including civilian killings, vehicle burnings, and abusive counter-insurgency operations.

The risk remains active. While some local agreements have eased movement restrictions in specific areas, recent developments indicate that coordinated JNIM–FLA operations continue to generate significant humanitarian consequences through displacement, access constraints, market disruptions, and the progressive isolation of northern and central regions. The humanitarian impact of the April escalation remains evident in Kidal and neighbouring regions. Food security conditions in Kidal are expected to deteriorate from Crisis (IPC Phase 3) to Emergency (IPC Phase 4) from June onwards as insecurity, military bombardments, reduced trade flows from Algeria, and the absence of escorted convoys further isolate the region during the lean season. Access to humanitarian assistance remains severely constrained, while worsening market shortages, high prices, and restrictions on livestock movements are reducing household access to food and income.
Displacement and service disruptions continue to increase humanitarian needs. WFP reported 2,328 newly displaced people from Kidal to Gao following the April crisis, while all 16 schools in Kidal remained closed through May, disrupting education for more than 2,900 students. At the same time, insecurity continues to affect key transport corridors and access to essential goods. Although a locally negotiated agreement led JNIM to lift its nearly two-year blockade of the road linking Bamako to Nara and Mourdiah, other areas remain affected by movement restrictions, insecurity, and fuel shortages. In Tombouctou, prolonged fuel shortages linked to JNIM's blockade have contributed to disruptions in electricity and water services, forcing residents to rely on limited alternative water sources. Similar disruptions to trade flows and fuel supplies continue to affect purchasing power and access to basic goods across northern and central Mali.
Over the next one to three months, continued JNIM–FLA pressure on transport corridors, urban supply chains, and contested territories is likely to sustain displacement, restrict humanitarian access, and worsen food insecurity, particularly in Kidal, Ménaka, Gao, and parts of Mopti and Tombouctou. While local agreements may temporarily reduce violence in some areas, they do not address the broader deterioration in state control, humanitarian access, and civilian protection conditions across northern and central Mali.

triggers.title: Expansion of coordinated JNIM–FLA operations
triggers.description: Coordinated attacks by JNIM and the FLA against military bases, urban centres, and strategic infrastructure may continue or expand into additional regions, increasing territorial contestation and exposing civilians to heightened insecurity. Although likely tactical and temporary, continued operational coordination between both actors could allow simultaneous attacks across multiple regions and increase pressure on Malian forces. Sustained cooperation may also increase pressure on transport corridors and urban areas, particularly around central and northern Mali, while complicating military operations and humanitarian access. Further attacks on strategic towns or military positions could increase insecurity in areas previously considered comparatively more stable.
triggers.objective: 100% completion would be reached if coordinated JNIM–FLA operations expand beyond current areas of activity and result in sustained attacks against additional strategic urban centres, transport corridors, or military installations across northern and central Mali.

triggers.title: Intensification of military operations and retaliatory violence
triggers.description: In response to the coordinated attacks, Malian forces and allied armed actors may increase military operations, aerial strikes, and security measures in contested areas. Expanded military deployments around strategic towns, transport corridors, and urban centres may increase movement restrictions and insecurity for civilians. Escalating confrontations and the militarisation of strategic urban centres and transport routes may increase protection risks for civilians, including displacement, restrictions on movement, and disruptions to humanitarian operations and access to essential services. Communities perceived as supporting rival armed actors may also face heightened risks of reprisals, arbitrary restrictions, or violence by conflict parties.
triggers.objective: 100% completion would be reached if expanded military operations and retaliatory violence result in sustained movement restrictions, significant civilian displacement, widespread protection incidents, or major disruptions to humanitarian access and essential services in conflict-affected areas.

title: El Niño-induced dry conditions in southern and central Mozambique and floods in the northern provinces increase humanitarian needs in 2026 and early 2027
riskType: New emerging risk
rationale: Climate projections indicate a high likelihood of El Niño conditions developing in July 2026 and persisting into the 2026/2027 rainy season, coinciding with Mozambique's main agricultural period. El Niño will drive contrasting rainfall patterns, with drier conditions in southern and central regions and wetter conditions in the north. The anticipated event is driven by abnormal warming of equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures, which disrupts global atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. El Niño typically brings below-normal rains in southern Mozambique and above-normal rains to the northern provinces, raising the likelihood of flooding and river overflow. Seasonal forecasts for the October–December period anticipate these typical El Niño patterns, indicating a moderate probability of above-average precipitation in the north and below-average precipitation in the south. The entire country is expected to experience above-average temperatures in July–December, which will compound dry conditions in the south and increase the risk of waterborne and vector-borne diseases in flood-exposed areas. Mozambique's high exposure to climate variability and reliance on rainfed agriculture further amplify vulnerability to climatic shocks. From September–October 2026, delayed or below-average precipitation in southern and central areas, combined with abnormally high temperatures, may affect land preparation and planting. If dry conditions continue through early 2027, crop yields and water availability may decrease, leading to a below-average maize, rice, millet, and sorghum harvest. At the same time, northern areas are likely to experience above-average precipitation, which may be beneficial to agriculture but also increases the risk of flooding, infrastructure damage, and displacement. These combined impacts are expected to increase humanitarian needs, particularly in food security, nutrition, WASH, and health.
expectedImpact: The anticipated El Niño during the 2026/2027 rainy season is expected to generate significant multisector humanitarian impacts across Mozambique, consistent with impacts observed during the 2023/2024 El Niño event. During that period, below-average rainfall and high temperatures in southern and central regions led to widespread drought, crop failure, and declining agricultural production, with national output losses and reduced yields concentrated in central and southern provinces. These conditions contributed to large-scale food insecurity, with up to 4.9 million people facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse conditions by early 2025. Similar patterns are expected in 2026/2027, with reduced rainfall and rising temperatures likely to limit soil moisture, reduce crop yields, and constrain water availability, particularly for subsistence households reliant on rainfed agriculture. This will likely translate into reduced food access, income losses, and increased malnutrition risk. Conversely, during the 2023/2024 El Niño, northern Mozambique experienced above-average rainfall and localised flooding, damaging crops and infrastructure and disrupting livelihoods. A similar flood risk is expected in northern provinces in 2026/2027, potentially causing infrastructure damage, market disruption, and heightened risk of waterborne diseases, including cholera. Impacts will likely be amplified in conflict-affected northern areas (Cabo Delgado, Nampula, Niassa), where displacement and limited access to services reduce coping capacity. Overall, El Niño is likely to simultaneously drive drought in the south and flooding in the north, increasing humanitarian needs across food security, WASH, health, and livelihoods, with the most severe impacts during the peak rainy season.

updates.text: The risk has further increased in September 2026 as forecasts indicate a strong to very strong El Niño from October 2026 to February 2027, with below-average rainfall expected across parts of southern Madagascar (Androy, Anosy, and Atsimo-Andrefana regions) during the October–November start of the rainy season. Assessments indicate that the lean season has already started earlier than usual in the Grand South, with poor households exhausting food stocks in September following below-average 2025/26 harvests and increasingly relying on markets and negative coping strategies. Conditions are expected to deteriorate further from October, with around 3.7 million people (11% of the analysed population) projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between October 2026 and February 2027, including nearly 426,000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). El Niño-related rainfall deficits could further reduce 2027 crop production and household incomes, particularly in the Grand South, increasing food insecurity and humanitarian needs through early 2027, though past El Niño events had limited effects on national paddy output.

The risk has worsened since July 2026 as forecasts indicate increasing confidence that a strong El Niño will persist through the 2026–2027 rainy season, raising the likelihood of drought in southern and central Mozambique and flooding in northern provinces. Humanitarian organisations and government stakeholders have intensified preparedness efforts, with anticipatory action triggers already activated in several districts owing to the heightened climate risk. Conflict-related displacement in Cabo Delgado province and funding shortfalls for humanitarian operations further compound existing vulnerabilities. In the short to medium term, affected households may face reduced agricultural production, declining food access, displacement, disease outbreaks, and increased needs across the food security, nutrition, health, and WASH sectors.

triggers.title: Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions
triggers.description:
Below-average rainfall and rising temperatures in southern and central regions: 
During El Niño events, large-scale atmospheric circulation shifts suppress moisture transport into southern Africa, reducing rainfall during the main cropping season. In southern and central Mozambique, this often results in prolonged dry spells, erratic rainfall distribution, and early cessation of rains rather than a complete absence of precipitation. At the same time, above-average temperatures increase evapotranspiration rates, accelerating the loss of soil moisture and surface water. This combination reduces water availability for domestic consumption, crops and livestock, heightens the risk of pasture degradation, and can lead to reduced agricultural yields or crop failure, particularly for rainfed smallholder farmers.

triggers.title: Above-average rainfall in northern provinces
triggers.description: El Niño conditions can enhance moisture inflow in parts of northern Mozambique, leading to above-average and more intense rainfall events. This increases the likelihood of river overflow, flash floods, and waterlogging, especially in low-lying and flood-prone districts. Saturated soils reduce infiltration and increase surface runoff, amplifying flood severity even during short periods of heavy rainfall. Flooding can damage homes, crops, and transport infrastructure, disrupt market access, and increase the risk of population displacement and waterborne diseases, further compounding humanitarian needs.

triggers.title: Delayed onset and irregular distribution of rains
triggers.description: El Niño is often associated with a late or erratic start to the rainy season, followed by uneven rainfall patterns throughout the season. In Mozambique, this disrupts the agricultural calendar, delaying planting and reducing the effective growing period for key crops such as maize. Intermittent dry spells during critical crop growth stages can further reduce yields. At the same time, unpredictable rainfall undermines farmers’ decision-making and increases the likelihood of replanting, leading to higher input costs and reduced resilience among households dependent on farming.

title: Sustained military pressure in Cabo Delgado drives Islamic State Mozambique attacks on less-exposed communities in Niassa and northern Nampula, causing localised displacement, abductions, and livelihood loss
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Islamic State Mozambique (ISM) activity in northern Mozambique has increasingly shifted towards mobile, small-group operations as a response to intensified military pressure from Mozambican security forces and their regional partners. Increased patrols, aerial surveillance, and continued counterinsurgency operations have reduced non-state armed groups' capacity to hold territory. As a result, ISM have increasingly dispersed from areas under intensified military pressure in Macomia district towards southern and western Cabo Delgado province. ISM have moved through Quissanga, Mecufi, and Meluco towards Ancuabe and Chiure districts, while other groups moved west towards Montepuez district and subsequently towards Niassa province. One group also crossed into Erati district in Nampula province.
Over the next six months, continued military pressure in Cabo Delgado is expected to further disperse ISM fighters towards areas with weaker security coverage. Remote forested areas and limited state presence in parts of Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, which have had some pockets of attacks, provide opportunities for small groups to move and conduct more attacks. ISM have increasingly targeted informal gold mining sites for looting and ransom, while attacks on vehicles and road users have generated additional income through extortion. In Niassa, the July–November hunting season also increases the presence of hunting camps, tourism operators, and vehicles in remote areas, creating potential high-value targets for ransom and material gains. If ISM establish a presence in Montepuez, Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, these activities could provide alternative sources of revenue and sustain their operations.
expectedImpact:
Protection risks are likely to increase through killings, abductions, family separation, property destruction, and restrictions on movement, while further operations by the Armed Defence Forces of Mozambique in newly affected areas could expose civilians to clashes, displacement, and disruption of access to livelihoods and services. The September attack in Marrupa already killed two people, abducted 11, and displaced about 2,700 people. Children face an additional risk of abduction and forced recruitment. Recent recruitment and use of children by non-state armed groups has been documented in northern Mozambique, including the abduction of three children in Cabo Delgado in February 2026.
Livelihoods are likely to deteriorate and food insecurity to increase as violence restricts access to farmland, markets, and labour opportunities. In 2025, Marrupa district, Niassa province, had an estimated 110,000 inhabitants, with smallholder agriculture an important source of food and income. Some households in the district were found to depend entirely on small-scale farming after previous climate shocks. Niassa had about 196,000 people in Crisis or worse (IPC Phase 3+) between October 2025 and March 2026, equivalent to 12% of its analysed population. Further violence, particularly ahead of the November lean season, could reduce household food stocks, interrupt agricultural activity, and increase market dependence. Disruption is particularly important during the July–November hunting season, which represents a critical seasonal driver of formal revenue and local livelihoods. A persistent ISM presence in Niassa may destabilise the local economy, forcing community displacement and restricting access to vital tourism-dependent livelihoods.
Health services could deteriorate if attacks damage facilities or insecurity prevents health workers and communities from reaching them. The Marrupa attack destroyed a health centre, demonstrating that health infrastructure can be directly affected by ISM attacks; this would remove already limited local capacity rather than necessarily indicating deliberate targeting of health services. In 2025, Niassa had 221 health facilities in total. Of these, four were higher-level referral hospitals: three secondary (district/rural/general) and one tertiary (provincial) hospital, while many communities in Mozambique already travel long distances to reach care. Further displacement and road insecurity could therefore interrupt routine, maternal, and child healthcare, as well as vaccination and emergency referrals.

triggers.title: Increased FADM pressure in northern Cabo Delgado
triggers.description: Continued military operations in Macomia, Muidumbe and surrounding areas could further fragment ISM groups and push fighters towards Quissanga, Meluco, Ancuabe, Chiúre, Montepuez and Niassa. ACLED has documented ISM groups moving south and west following increased state-force pressure in the Catupa area, while subsequent FADM operations also pushed fighters towards Montepuez and the Niassa border.

triggers.title: July–November hunting season increases the concentration of high-value targets in remote areas:
triggers.description: The hunting season in Niassa runs through November, bringing increased activity by hunting camps, tourism operators and associated personnel in remote areas of the Niassa Reserve. This creates a seasonal concentration of people, vehicles and other high-value assets in areas with limited security coverage. The 3 September ISM attack on a hunting camp in Marrupa occurred during the current hunting season, indicating that this seasonal activity can create opportunities for NSAG operations in Niassa.

triggers.title: Changes in the coverage of Rwandan and other external security forces
triggers.description: A significant reduction, redeployment or change in operational coverage by Rwandan or other external security forces in Cabo Delgado could create additional space for ISM activity and facilitate movement into southern Cabo Delgado and neighbouring provinces. Rwanda was still rotating personnel into Cabo Delgado in July 2026, while Mozambique has continued to describe the Rwandan deployment as an important component of counter-insurgency operations.

title: Military operations to secure the Dawei Special Economic Zone cause further forced displacement and severe protection risks in Dawei district, Tanintharyi region
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
By 28 August 2026, an estimated 700–1,000 military personnel were conducting clearance operations around the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Yebyu township after a late-June order to protect the strategic projects. Since 9 July, fighting, raids, arson, looting, arbitrary arrests, and killings have displaced more than 4,500 people from eight Nabule villages. Renewed fighting near the SEZ from 21–22 August caused further civilian displacement. More than 2,000 people were displaced from ten villages in Thayetchaung township in August.
The concentration of military deployments around the project area, following orders to protect strategic infrastructure and agreements to revive the project, indicates that the operation is intended to secure the SEZ. The SEZ is a long-stalled port and industrial zone planned to include a deep-sea port, coal-fired power plant, oil refinery, and liquefied natural gas facilities. The risk is more immediate because Myanmar and Russia revived the project in 2025, signed a June 2026 power plant agreement, and included the Dawei port, refinery, and power plant in their August Moscow agreements. The timing of these deals and the deployment, alongside clashes with the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) near Wet Chaung, makes control of the project area a current strategic objective rather than a remote development scenario.
Over the next six months, military efforts to secure the SEZ are likely to include attempts to control Highway 8, the main north–south route through Tanintharyi, and the Dawei–Htee Khee road, which connects the project area through Myitta to the Thailand border. These routes are important for moving troops and supplies and would support future port and SEZ operations. Continued resistance activities by the KNLA, National Unity Government-affiliated People’s Defence Forces, and other local resistance groups operating in and around the Dawei SEZ could trigger further military sweeps, preventing safe returns and causing new and repeated displacement. Prolonged separation from homes, farms, and plantations will reduce food production and household income, increasing dependence on markets and host communities and worsening food, shelter, and health needs.
expectedImpact:
Further military operations are likely to cause rapid and repeated displacement from villages around the SEZ and its access routes. Households may separate, with some members remaining to protect homes, plantations, and livestock while others seek safety elsewhere. This could complicate family reunification, displacement tracking, and access to assistance. People travelling through checkpoints or returning to their villages will face increased risks of detention, forced recruitment, and exposure to indirect fire.
Families sheltering in forests, plantations, or incomplete structures will face worsening shelter, water, sanitation, and health conditions, particularly during the remainder of the monsoon season. Limited transport and healthcare access may delay treatment, maternal care, and medical referrals.
Food security and livelihoods will worsen as farmers and plantation workers lose access to land, stored food, tools, livestock, and markets. An estimated 877,000 people in Tanintharyi already require humanitarian assistance in 2026, with needs classified as catastrophic (Severity 5) in Launglon and extreme (Severity 4) in Dawei, Thayetchaung, and Yebyu townships. Road insecurity, checkpoints, fuel scarcity, and controls on transported goods may further raise prices and restrict the delivery of food and relief. Host families will absorb additional costs while also facing disrupted local trade.
If physical implementation of the SEZ resumes, temporary displacement could become prolonged. Security perimeters, land demarcation, housing destruction, and missing documentation may prevent returns or pressure affected households to accept relocation or compensation. As operations around the SEZ overlap with wider military activity across Dawei district, newly displaced people may be scattered across different locations and recorded under separate incidents. This could delay verification of their numbers, locations, and needs, increasing the risk that some displaced communities, particularly those moving repeatedly or staying outside formal sites, may be missed during assessments and receive limited or irregular assistance.
Humanitarian access is likely to remain severely constrained as fighting and military checkpoints restrict roads into the SEZ area and limit the movement of food, medicine, shelter materials, and evacuation support. In July, three Burmese aid volunteers were detained while evacuating residents of Kamauk Chaung and later found killed after being used as human shields. This incident may deter grassroots responders from reaching displaced families. Civilians travelling between villages and displacement locations or returning to collect belongings, harvest crops, or tend to livestock will also face heightened risks of arrest, killing, forced recruitment, and use as human shields.

updates.text: The risk increased in September as military operations expanded across Launglon, Long Lone, Thayetchaung, and Yebyu townships and along Highway 8. In late September, troops advanced into Thit Taw Taung in Yebyu and Kyauk Sin in Launglon. Operations in Long Lone between 8–10 September killed four civilians and displaced nearly 5,000 people. In Yebyu, increased troop deployments, checkpoints, and questioning restricted civilians’ access to plantations and workplaces, while reports of civilians being forced to guide troops or act as human shields indicate heightened protection risks. Since late September, flooding and landslides have compounded these impacts by damaging roads and communications. Continued military activity has constrained displacement and evacuation, while blocked roads and limited access to machinery have delayed humanitarian assistance to villages isolated by floodwater and landslides. The combination of conflict and natural hazards is likely to increase displacement, restrict access to livelihoods and essential services, and prolong humanitarian access constraints.

triggers.title: Military reinforcement and establishment of permanent positions in the SEZ
triggers.description: ·The military reportedly controls Yebyu town and some SEZ compounds, while the wider Nabule area remains contested. The deployment of additional battalions, construction of fortified positions and roadblocks, increased patrols, land clearance, or engineering surveys around Nabule, Wet Chaung, and the deep-sea port site would indicate plans to establish a sustained security perimeter.

triggers.title: Coordinated resistance offensive against strategic military positions
triggers.description: A coordinated offensive by KNLA Brigade 4 and allied resistance groups to capture or encircle military positions near the SEZ, Highway 8 or the Myitta–Htee Khee route could trigger a large military counteroffensive involving additional troops and artillery, drone, air or naval support. If the offensive targets positions south of Yebyu or along the border route, the resulting military response could extend into Thayetchaung, the Dawei East Forest and Myitta, increasing civilian casualties and displacement across a wider area.

triggers.title: Resumption of physical work at the SEZ
triggers.description: The deployment of technical or construction teams and heavy machinery, renewed land measurement, boundary marking or site clearance, or work on the port, power plant, refinery, LNG facilities or road to Thailand would indicate a shift from political agreements to implementation. If accompanied by increased military deployments or security restrictions, these developments would increase the risk of eviction, land loss and prolonged displacement.

title: Escalation of inter-group conflict between Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and Islamic State Sahel Province in western Niger leads to increased violence against civilians and displacement
riskType: New emerging risk
rationale:
In early April 2026, the Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) attacked a Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) position in Tillabéri, marking the first reported direct confrontation between the two groups in Niger after years of rivalry concentrated in Mali and Burkina Faso. Tillabéri is already one of the most affected areas in the central Sahel, where violence against civilians, displacement, and weak state presence have created acute protection risks. Tillabéri recorded the highest level of civilian targeting across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger in 2025, with over 1,200 of Niger’s 1,939 civilian fatalities occurring there, primarily attributed to ISSP, followed by JNIM and the Nigerien military.
The risk of escalation is linked to the geographic expansion of JNIM–ISSP competition into western Niger, where both groups are increasingly competing for territorial influence, recruitment networks, road axes, and local economies. Recent attacks on military installations in Tahoua city, including the Base Aérienne 401 and the 42nd battalion headquarters in March 2026, indicate that insecurity is increasingly affecting strategic urban and military locations beyond the main rural border areas of Tillabéri. These developments have already disrupted humanitarian operations, with UNHAS flights temporarily suspended because of insecurity and repercussions on humanitarian access.
Over the next six months, escalation of JNIM–ISSP clashes in western Niger could mirror patterns seen in Mali and Burkina Faso, where rivalry expansion led to heightened violence against civilians, mass displacement, and further erosion of state control. Armed group competition and pressure on key road axes will likely expand attacks into previously less-affected communes and towns in western Niger, leading to a deterioration in civilian security and access to services. Both groups may intensify targeting of populations perceived to support rivals, particularly rural communities in contested border areas of Tillabéri, as well as displaced and host communities, leaving civilians vulnerable to crossfire, accusations of collaboration, and illegal taxation. Tillabéri’s existing high baseline of civilian harm, combined with weak state presence, protracted displacement, and fragile livelihoods, could amplify the impact of further escalation. New displacement, exacerbated food insecurity, and deepened humanitarian access constraints are likely as groups compete for recruitment and resources in this strategic border zone.
expectedImpact:
An escalation of JNIM–ISSP clashes in western Niger would likely increase civilian casualties, displacement, and protection risks in areas already facing severe humanitarian needs. Tillabéri experienced a significant deterioration in security in the first quarter of 2026, with over 92,900 forcibly displaced people recorded in key departments and acute protection risks including killings, abductions, gender-based violence, and child protection concerns. Tahoua is also highly vulnerable, hosting 80,475 refugees, 65,892 IDPs, 10,597 returnees, and 52,805 asylum-seekers awaiting registration.

Further inter-group rivalry could expose communities in contested areas to reprisals for perceived collaboration with rival groups or state forces, while illegal taxation, extortion, and movement restrictions may further erode livelihoods and household coping capacities. Increased insecurity may also heighten risks of child recruitment, forced marriage, and other negative coping mechanisms, particularly among displaced and conflict-affected communities.

Humanitarian access constraints are also likely to worsen. In Tahoua, 582,061 people were estimated to be in need in 2025, with 40–50% located in hard-to-access areas. The imposition of armed escorts has already reduced operational capacity, with only one in five humanitarian missions carried out, while escort costs and administrative restrictions continue to limit the frequency of interventions.

Service disruption could aggravate already severe humanitarian conditions. Nationally, 3.9 million people, including 2.6 million children, require urgent humanitarian assistance, while 2.4 million people are projected to face severe food insecurity. Niger’s health and education systems are already under pressure, with 1.8 million people in need of health assistance and 1,097 schools non-functional, affecting 93,676 children. A further deterioration in Tillabéri and Tahoua would likely deepen protection needs, disrupt markets and basic services, and leave more conflict-affected communities under-assisted.

updates.text: The risk increased during September as armed groups are expanding and consolidating overlapping areas of operation. Armed group activity continued to place pressure on Nigerien forces in western Niger during the second half of September, although no significant direct clashes between the Support Group for Islam and Muslims (JNIM) and Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) were reported. On 26 September, two attacks attributed to Islamic State militants targeted Nigerien security forces near Abala in Tillabéri region and at Dabagu in Konni department, Tahoua region, killing 50–57 soldiers and gendarmes. The simultaneous attacks across two regions indicate ISSP's continued capacity to conduct high-impact operations against state forces beyond its core areas in Tillabéri. Violence also continued in Dosso region, with attacks reported in Dioundiou department during the second half of September, reinforcing indications of the southward expansion of armed group activity. While these developments increase pressure on security forces and confirm the continued geographic expansion of armed groups, there is not yet clear evidence of an escalation in direct JNIM–ISSP confrontation in Niger.

The risk has deteriorated as sustained operations of Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and Islamic State – Sahel Province (ISSP) across western Niger in August 2026 further weakened the State’s ability to maintain security in rural areas and increased civilian exposure to violence, displacement, and movement restrictions. Attacks across Diffa, Dosso, Maradi, and Tillabéri regions between 21–25 August, including JNIM’s seizure of a military post in Bangoume commune, Tillabéri, and an ISSP assault on a gendarmerie post in Tessa commune, Dosso, that killed at least 18 gendarmes, indicate a widening operational footprint beyond established hotspots. The coup attempt on 29 August, linked partly to military discontent over mounting casualties, further raises concerns over the security forces’ capacity to contain armed-group activity. In Tillabéri, where more than 330,000 people are displaced, insecurity is contributing to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity through January 2027, with Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes projected among the most asset-depleted displaced households.

Western Niger has become the main area of competition between Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Islamic State in the Sahel Province (ISSP) as both groups intensify operations to expand and consolidate territorial influence. In June 2026, ISSP launched large-scale attacks against military positions in Inates and Banibangou, while JNIM expanded its presence through coordinated attacks targeting Niamey Airport and several localities along the Niger–Burkina Faso border. Although direct confrontations between the groups remain limited, their competition is contributing to more frequent and higher-intensity attacks against military positions and strategic infrastructure, further destabilising Tillabéri region. Continued insecurity is driving displacement, disrupting livelihoods and markets, and restricting humanitarian access. By mid-July, around 230,000 people had been newly displaced since the beginning of 2026, while Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity is expected to persist across conflict-affected areas of Tillabéri until at least January 2027. Attacks near Tera in July indicate that the operational tempo remains high, suggesting western Niger will remain the centre of JNIM–ISSP competition in the coming months.

triggers.title: Increased frequency of direct clashes between JNIM and ISSP in western Niger
triggers.description: Reports of repeated armed confrontations between JNIM and ISSP in Tillabéri and Tahoua indicate a shift towards sustained inter-group rivalry and territorial contestation. An increase in the frequency, scale, or geographic spread of these clashes would signal a deterioration in the security environment and a higher likelihood of violence against civilians and displacement in affected areas.
triggers.objective: Yes: At least 3–5 reported clashes per month between JNIM and ISSP in Tillabéri and/or Tahoua, or evidence of sustained clashes over a period of 2–3 consecutive weeks.

triggers.title: Increased targeting of civilians in contested areas
triggers.description: Reports of killings, abductions, or threats against civilians in areas where JNIM and ISSP are competing for influence, particularly in Tillabéri and Tahoua. Increased violence against civilians may reflect retaliatory dynamics and efforts by both groups to assert territorial control, increasing protection risks and displacement.
triggers.objective: Yes: civilian casualties per month linked to armed group activity in Tillabéri/Tahoua, or a clear increasing trend over 2–3 consecutive months.

triggers.title: Expansion of inter-group violence into new areas
triggers.description: Attacks or presence of JNIM or ISSP reported in areas previously less affected, including new localities in Tahoua or neighbouring regions. Geographic expansion would indicate a widening scope of inter-group rivalry and increasing insecurity beyond established hotspots.
triggers.objective: Yes: Confirmed presence or attacks by JNIM and/or ISSP in at least 2–3 new administrative areas (departments or communes) beyond previously affected zones.

triggers.title: Increase in displacement from western Niger
triggers.description: Rising displacement flows from Tillabéri and Tahoua linked to insecurity and inter-group clashes. Increased displacement would indicate worsening protection conditions and reduced population resilience in affected areas.
triggers.objective: Yes: An increase of newly displaced people within a short period (1–2 months) linked to insecurity in affected regions.

title: Post-mutiny divisions in Niger's army enable JNIM and ISSP expansion across Tillabéri, Tahoua, and Dosso, driving displacement and restricting humanitarian access
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: The 28–29 August mutiny in Niamey exposed growing divisions within Niger's armed forces that are directly connected to the counterinsurgency front line. Officers and units involved were based in Ouallam and Tera in Tillabéri region and in Dosso region, while grievances included mounting casualties in fighting the Support Group for Islam and Muslims (JNIM) and Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP), as well as perceived preferential treatment of the better-equipped Presidential Guard. Subsequent arrests of soldiers from special forces units in Tillabéri and changes in senior military leadership indicate that the mutiny is already affecting forces deployed in conflict-affected western regions. These divisions are emerging as non-state armed groups intensify pressure across western Niger. Violence remains concentrated in Tillabéri and northern Tahoua, while increasing attacks in Dosso indicate southward expansion. Additional deployments around Niamey, further arrests or command changes, and greater reliance on forces for regime protection could reduce military presence or operational capacity in conflict hotspots, creating additional space for armed groups. Over the next 3–6 months, JNIM and ISSP could exploit reduced or disrupted security force capacity to intensify attacks in existing hotspots in Tillabéri and northern Tahoua and expand their operating space further into Dosso. Increased violence and military operations would generate additional displacement, disrupt livelihoods and access to basic services, and further constrain humanitarian access.
expectedImpact: Displacement is expected to increase in Tillabéri, northwestern Tahoua, and areas of Dosso affected by expanding insecurity. More than 85,000 people were displaced in Tillabéri alone between October 2025 and early 2026, illustrating the scale of population movements that recent insecurity can generate. If insecurity intensifies over the next 3–6 months, displacement would remain predominantly local, towards departmental centres and safer host communities, including Tera and its outskirts, Tahoua town and Tchintabaraden, and Dogondoutchi from affected areas of Dosso. Populations remaining in areas where ISSP consolidates or expands its influence would face heightened protection risks associated with coercive control. In Tillabéri and northern Tahoua, this could include increased taxation and livestock seizures, ultimatums to leave villages, restrictions on movement and access to livelihoods, alongside direct attacks against civilians. These practices could further erode household assets and contribute to additional displacement. Insecurity during the October–January harvest and post-harvest period could deepen food insecurity in Tillabéri and northwestern Tahoua, where IPC 3 outcomes are already expected through January 2027 and some displaced households face IPC 4. Reduced access to fields could leave crops unharvested, accelerate household stock depletion, and increase earlier-than-usual market dependence, potentially resulting in an earlier or deeper lean season. In Dosso, expanding insecurity could disrupt agricultural production and cross-border trade, particularly around Dioundiou and Gaya and along routes connecting Niger with Benin and Nigeria. Reduced trade flows could constrain market supply and increase transport costs, including for markets supplying Dosso and Niamey. Humanitarian access could deteriorate along routes serving Tera, Ouallam, Tillabéri, and Banibangou, and along the Niamey–Dosso road, disrupting humanitarian deliveries and reducing the regularity and geographical coverage of assistance.

triggers.title: Further military dissent, purges, or command disruption:
triggers.description: Further mutinies, arrests, dismissals, or changes within the Nigerien armed forces could deepen internal divisions and disrupt command continuity and operational coordination. The replacement of armed forces chief of staff Moussa Salaou Barmou and other senior command changes following the August mutiny indicate ongoing restructuring, although their effect on military effectiveness remains unclear. Further changes affecting commanders or units deployed in conflict-affected western regions would increase the likelihood of reduced counterinsurgency capacity.

triggers.title: Diversion of security capacity towards regime protection
triggers.description: Increased deployment of Nigerien forces and allied security partners to protect strategic sites, monitor military personnel, or respond to further threats against the government could divert personnel, intelligence, logistical capacity, and other resources from counterinsurgency operations. The government's reliance on Russia's Africa Corps to suppress the August mutiny and previous reinforcement of the security apparatus in Niamey indicate heightened concern over threats to regime security.

triggers.title: Disruption or blockade of strategic supply routes by non-state armed groups.
triggers.description: JNIM or ISSP attacks, checkpoints, or blockades affecting major routes connecting Niamey with Tillabéri, Téra, Ouallam, Banibangou, or Dosso would indicate growing ability to isolate state positions and population centres, restrict military resupply and civilian movement, and constrain humanitarian access.
triggers.objective: the number of major routes connecting Niamey with Tillabéri, Téra, Ouallam, Banibangou, or Dosso affected by sustained JNIM or ISSP blockades or disruptions. The threshold is at least one strategic route experiencing sustained disruption that significantly restricts civilian movement, military resupply, or humanitarian access.

title: Permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line before the Israeli elections increases displacement and humanitarian access constraints
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
There is a high probability that Israeli forces will formally declare and physically enclose a permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line in the period leading up to Israel's October 2026 parliamentary elections, progressively reducing the territory accessible to civilians and humanitarian responders.
Since the 10 October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli forces have steadily expanded their military footprint beyond the initial demarcation line through tank advances, repeated evacuation orders, the construction of defensive positions, and localised operations. The Israeli-controlled area had expanded from 53% of Gaza Strip at the ceasefire to 64.9% by June 2026, with the trend notably intensifying late into the month. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data reports that events reflecting Yellow Line expansion and associated military movements increased from an average of fewer than four events per month between October 2025 and mid-June 2026 to 22 events between 18 June and 17 July 2026, a more than fivefold increase.

During the same period, activity by the Shuja’iyya Popular Defense Forces led by Rami Hilles, an anti-Hamas Palestinian armed group operating with Israeli support, also increased. Between 30 June and 9 July, the group carried out three recorded incidents targeting IDP camps in Gaza city's At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya neighbourhoods, including reported abductions and raids, indicating increasingly complex security dynamics around the expanding Yellow Line.

The period preceding Israel's October 2026 elections has a high probability of reinforcing this trajectory rather than prompting a fundamental shift in military strategy. With far-right coalition partners Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism continuing to advocate expanding Israeli control over Gaza and negotiations on a durable ceasefire and post-conflict governance remaining stalled, the Likud-led caretaker government, in place since the Knesset dissolved on 17 July 2026, will very probably prioritise maintaining operational momentum in Gaza while avoiding the political and military risks associated with a large-scale offensive.

Territorial expansion is expected to continue through a combination of military and engineering measures that progressively transform temporary military positions into more permanent areas of control. Israeli forces are likely to continue advancing the Yellow Line through localised incursions supported by repeated evacuation orders, the demolition of buildings and agricultural land, and the construction of additional military infrastructure, including outposts, surveillance positions, access roads, trenches, and earthen barriers. Recent satellite imagery indicates that Israel has already constructed more than 23km of earth berms and trenches along parts of the Yellow Line, creating a fortified corridor that extends across central Gaza and, in some locations, beyond the original ceasefire demarcation. These measures are likely to be accompanied by the continued expansion of military exclusion zones and restrictions on civilian movement, allowing Israeli forces to consolidate control without undertaking a single large-scale offensive.
expectedImpact:
If this risk materialises, humanitarian conditions will deteriorate most acutely in areas adjacent to the expanding Yellow Line, particularly eastern Gaza city (including At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya), the Netzarim corridor in central Gaza, eastern Deir Al Balah, and northern Khan Younis. These areas may be the most affected because they lie along the current trajectory of Israeli territorial expansion and have experienced repeated military operations, evacuation orders, and engineering activities since late June 2026. Continued territorial consolidation would further reduce the already-limited areas available for civilians, increasing overcrowding in displacement sites and placing additional pressure on humanitarian service delivery.

Additional displacement would increase shelter needs at a time when humanitarian capacity is declining; the number of families receiving shelter assistance fell by 37% between May–June 2026 because of funding shortages and access restrictions.

Humanitarian access is highly likely to become increasingly constrained as the expanding Yellow Line reduces humanitarian operational space and fragments access routes. Additional military exclusion zones, fortifications, and engineering works will require more frequent coordination with Israeli authorities, limit access to communities near the evolving front line, and force humanitarian responders to rely on fewer approved corridors. This is expected to delay aid deliveries, hinder needs assessments, and limit infrastructure repairs.

Food security and livelihoods will probably deteriorate further from already critical levels. Between April–June 2026, 59% of Gaza's population faced Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse food insecurity, including around 212,000 people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) conditions. Further expansion of the Yellow Line would reduce access to agricultural land and remaining livelihood opportunities while restricting humanitarian food deliveries and market access. This would increase reliance on aid and deepen acute food insecurity.

Health and WASH conditions are likely to worsen from an already-overstretched baseline. Health facilities continue to face severe supply shortages, while 63% of assessed households receive less than 6L of water per person per day. The expansion of the Yellow Line would further restrict humanitarian access for medical referrals, infrastructure repairs, and supply deliveries, increasing pressure on health services and the risk of waterborne disease outbreaks and preventable deaths.

updates.text: The risk has deteriorated during August 2026 ahead of the 27 October Israeli elections, as Israeli military control continues to consolidate across Gaza. Further westward advancement of the Yellow Line into eastern Middle Area, Gaza city, and Khan Younis, alongside Israel’s approval of the Green Rafah infrastructure project in eastern Rafah under military supervision, indicates that temporary military positions are increasingly becoming permanent areas of control. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of the US-backed 15-point road map on 8 August, with Jared Kushner subsequently confirming that implementation was contingent on full Hamas disarmament, has reduced prospects for diplomatic measures that could constrain this consolidation before the elections. The expansion is already affecting humanitarian operations, with Yellow Line advances triggering evacuation and shelter-in-place orders affecting more than ten UNRWA premises, indicating that further territorial consolidation is likely to compound existing access constraints and accelerate the deterioration of humanitarian operational capacity.

triggers.title: Israeli decision formalising further territorial expansion
triggers.description: The Israeli Security Cabinet or Ministry of Defense formally authorises a further advance of the "Yellow Line" or designates areas east of it as permanent military exclusion zones or closed military areas.

triggers.title: Breakdown of post-conflict governance negotiations
triggers.description: Public suspension or collapse of negotiations on Hamas disarmament and post-conflict governance, including the reversal of the 26 July 2026 cabinet decision permitting the initial deployment of the International Stabilisation Force.

triggers.title: Further increase in "Yellow Line" expansion activity
triggers.description: ACLED records "Yellow Line" expansion and associated military-movement events exceeding the June–July 2026 baseline of 22 events per month, indicating an acceleration of territorial consolidation.

triggers.title: Expansion of large-scale evacuation order
triggers.description: Israeli authorities issue new evacuation orders covering entire neighbourhoods adjacent to the "Yellow Line", including Zeitoun, At Tuffah, Shujaiyya, eastern Deir al Balah, or northern Rafah, signalling preparations for further military expansion.

title: Accelerated implementation of the E1 settlement plan results in demolitions, displacement of Bedouin communities, and access constraints
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The E1 settlement plan is a longstanding Israeli initiative that was revived in July 2025 after four years of suspension and approved for advancement by the Israeli Government on 20 August 2025. The plan aims to expand Ma’ale Adumim municipality and create a continuous built-up area between the Israeli settlements and Jerusalem city. Its implementation could further fragment the West Bank, particularly by disrupting geographic contiguity between central and southern areas, and increase the likelihood of severing East Jerusalem from the rest of the occupied West Bank. Its advancement could accelerate the displacement of entire Bedouin communities in the area, generating additional humanitarian needs.
Implementation has accelerated in 2026. In August, Israel issued a tender for 1,234 housing units in E1, followed on 17 September by a further 2,167 units, bringing the total to 3,401. Bidding on the 2,167-unit tender was scheduled to open on 25 October, two days before Israel's 27 October parliamentary elections.
Government efforts to advance the tenders before the election could accelerate implementation of the approved plan and trigger a faster-paced displacement. The awarding of tenders would allow the Israeli Government to move faster towards infrastructure works and construction, making the project more difficult for a future government to reverse. Implementation could accelerate if the tender process proceeds despite the postponement and the current Government retains power after the election. Court challenges or an election outcome that produces a government less supportive of E1 could, however, delay further implementation.
expectedImpact:
Implementation of E1 is likely to increase displacement among the approximately 4,000 Palestinians living in 18 Bedouin and herding communities in and around the designated area, through demolitions, evictions, and loss of access to land. Displacement is already being reported near the designated area, with 66 people displaced in South ‘Anata and Tublas between 8–17 September. E1 implementation could increase the frequency and geographic scope of such incidents as construction and associated infrastructure works progress.
Construction of settlements, roads, and related infrastructure could restrict movement between Palestinian communities and reduce access to East Jerusalem, markets, health services, and other essential services such as education. In the first half of 2026, 224 education-related incidents affected 152 schools and 20,450 students across the West Bank, of which 122 involved access restrictions, illustrating the extent to which movement restrictions already disrupt essential services. E1 implementation could create additional checkpoints, road closures, or rerouting around construction areas and settlement infrastructure.
E1 implementation could reduce access to grazing land, agricultural areas, and water resources, undermining the livestock-based livelihoods of affected Bedouin communities and increasing dependence on humanitarian assistance. On 19 July, settlers damaged water pipelines serving approximately 200 residents of Nkheila Bedouin community, restricted access to grazing areas, and took over the nearby Ein Rawabi spring, a key livestock water source. Further loss or fragmentation of grazing areas could reduce livestock holdings and household income and accelerate livelihood displacement.
Protection risks are likely to increase through greater exposure to settler violence, harassment, demolitions, and movement restrictions as settlement construction expands. More than 1,600 settler attacks affecting 275 Palestinian communities were recorded between January and September 2026. In E1-affected communities, implementation could increase encounters between settlers, Palestinians, and security forces, while demolitions and restrictions on access to land and services could expose Palestinians to forced displacement, family separation, and psychosocial distress.

triggers.title: Implementation of E1 tender awards before the elections
triggers.description: Progress of the E1 tenders, including any reversal of the Attorney General's postponement, before or after 27 October, could move the plan from approval towards physical implementation and make it more difficult for a future government to reverse.

triggers.title: Post-election government commitment
triggers.description: If the current government retains power and continues to support E1, it could accelerate planning approvals, infrastructure works, and construction.

title: El Niño-driven agricultural losses and water shortages in the Philippines increase food security, WASH, and health needs
riskType: New emerging risk
rationale:
The Philippines faces an increasing risk of El Niño-driven drought, potentially triggering water shortages, agricultural losses, and heat stress in the coming months. El Niño conditions are already present in the tropical Pacific, with sea surface temperature anomalies reaching the +0.5° C threshold in May 2026; most models indicate an over 80% probability of full development, persisting until early 2027 at strong to very strong intensity.
Seasonal forecasts anticipate below-average precipitation across central and southern regions from July–September, extending nationwide from October. The provinces likely to be affected are Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Kalinga, La Union, Mountain Province, Nueva Ecija, Nueva Vizcaya, Pangasinan, Quirino, and Tarlac. Temperatures are forecast above seasonal averages nationwide from July–December. This is likely to produce a poor monsoon season (May–October), vital for maize and rice production, affecting both rain-fed and irrigated crops. Main season rice, harvested in December, accounts for 60% of domestic production.
The Philippines has experienced 12 major drought events since 1968. It is estimated that agricultural drought caused approximately 20 million metric tons of crop losses between 1980–2020. Between July 2023 and April 2024, El Niño-related dry conditions affected multiple provinces, causing agricultural losses, water shortages, and livelihood disruptions. The Department of Social Welfare and Development reported thousands of farming households affected by prolonged dry spells, with losses in some provinces reaching hundreds of millions of pesos. This event also drove extreme heat, school disruptions, and mounting pressure on water and food systems – illustrating how El Niño can rapidly become a multisector humanitarian crisis for affected communities.
In the next one to three months, primary concerns include localised rainfall deficits, water stress, and heat-related impacts, particularly in affected agricultural zones. Over the next three to six months, if El Niño strengthens as projected, drought conditions could intensify significantly, leading to reduced crop yields, livestock stress, water shortages, rising food prices, and worsening livelihood pressures. This may increase humanitarian needs in the WASH, food security, and health sectors, particularly in already-vulnerable rural communities.
expectedImpact:
Below-normal rainfall and above-average temperatures are likely to reduce soil moisture, lower reservoir levels, and disrupt irrigation systems, particularly in drought-prone agricultural areas. This may lead to reduced crop yields, livestock stress, and lower household income among farming communities, increasing food insecurity and coping strategies with potentially harmful consequences. Water shortages may affect both domestic consumption and agricultural production, increasing demand for water rationing or emergency water supply interventions.
Heat-related health risks, including dehydration and heat stress, may also increase, particularly among older people, children, outdoor workers, and communities with limited access to cooling or clean water. Indirect economic effects may further worsen humanitarian conditions. If disruptions to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz trigger higher global fuel prices, transport and agricultural production costs may rise significantly. This could contribute to higher food prices, reduced market access, and higher costs for essential goods, compounding El Niño-related livelihood pressures. Combined climate and economic shocks could disproportionately affect poor and rural households with limited coping capacity.

updates.text: The risk has increased as El Niño strengthens, with impacts on agriculture and water availability already reported in parts of the Philippines. A strong to very strong El Niño is expected to persist through the first half of 2027 and may peak before the end of 2026. In Davao region, 4,447 farmers have been affected, with approximately 4,791 hectares of crops damaged and PHP 444 million in losses since El Niño emerged in August. Rice production has been particularly affected. In Agusan del Sur province, low river levels, cracked rice fields, dry-spell damage to corn plantations, and critically low water supplies at the provincial government centre were reported in September. Further intensification could increase crop losses and water shortages, reducing agricultural income and access to water among farming communities. These impacts could increase food security and WASH needs over the coming months. The nationwide scale of humanitarian needs remains unclear.

The risk is active and stable, as during July 2026, weak-to-moderate El Niño conditions developed in the tropical Pacific, marking the onset of the anticipated event. Updated climate projections indicate a 97% probability that El Niño would persist through the first half of 2027. These projections indicate that El Niño will intensify over the coming months, with a 57% probability of strong conditions from July–September 2026 and an 81% probability of very strong conditions from October–December 2026 and from November 2026 to January 2027. Forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of drought and below-normal rainfall in parts of the Philippines from late 2026, with potential impacts on agricultural production and water availability. Until July, however, there remained no evidence of the developing El Niño causing significant agricultural losses, widespread water shortages, food price increases, or increased humanitarian needs.

triggers.title: Below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures
triggers.description: El Niño typically suppresses rainfall across the Philippines while also contributing to above-average temperatures. During the monsoon season, it also contributes to irregular rainfall distribution, characterized by intermittent dry spells and uneven precipitation.  Reduced or unheavenly distributed rainfall, combined with high temperatures, increases evapotranspiration, accelerating the depletion of soil moisture, while reduced precipitation affect surface and groundwater reserves. This can significantly reduce water availability for domestic consumption, irrigation, and livestock, particularly in drought-prone and agriculture-dependent provinces. Prolonged heat and moisture stress can also damage crops during critical growth stages, reduce agricultural productivity, and increase heat-related health risks, especially among affected rural households and outdoor workers.

title: Escalating violence between the Sudan People's Liberation Movement and the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-in-Opposition reignites civil war, driving mass displacement and service collapse
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The collapse of the 2018 revitalized peace agreement and the disbandment of the unity government have dramatically increased the risk of South Sudan sliding back into full-scale civil conflict. The March 2025 arrest of First Vice President Riek Machar of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition by President Salva Kiir has reignited ethnically charged fighting between Dinka and Nuer armed forces, with clashes already concentrated in Jonglei and Upper Nile states. Up to 300,000 newly displaced people add to the approximately two million already internally displaced and over ten million – two-thirds of the population – requiring some form of humanitarian assistance, including 7.5 million projected to face food insecurity during the April–July lean season. South Sudan has suffered from chronic violence since independence. The collapse of the peace framework ahead of elections, accompanied by the re-emergence of organised, ethnically mobilised armed groups, represents the risk of a return to full-scale civil war.
Several factors increase the likelihood of deterioration into civil war. The taking and retaking of Akobo signals an escalation beyond the fragmented, subnational violence that characterised the 2018–2024 period, with organised armed groups now contesting territory at a scale not seen since the first civil war. The mobilisation of Nuer armed groups, including the White Army, suggests this is a coordinated insurgency with the capacity to sustain prolonged fighting. Uganda's continued deployment of troops in support of Kiir's Government risks drawing the conflict into a broader regional confrontation, and spillover from Sudan and Ethiopia could further destabilise border areas. Over 1.36 million people have already arrived in South Sudan from Sudan since April 2023, with services in border areas stretched to breaking point; an additional 380,000 arrivals are projected by the end of 2026. The planned December 2026 elections, already twice postponed, will intensify political competition and may become a flashpoint for renewed violence, whether they proceed or are cancelled again.
expectedImpact: A return to full-scale civil war would rapidly overwhelm an already critically degraded humanitarian system. New displacement on the scale of the 2013–2018 civil war – when nearly half the population was uprooted – would exhaust regional absorption capacity, with Sudan at war and Ethiopia far from stable. As during the last civil war, secondary displacement flows towards North Africa and across the Mediterranean are likely. Famine risk, currently confined to Luakpiny/Nasir and Fangak, would spread rapidly as access collapses across conflict-affected areas. The established pattern of aid weaponisation would intensify; already, flight restrictions have suspended humanitarian flights to Akobo, Lankien, and Pieri, the bombing of the Médecins Sans Frontières Lankien hospital in February 2026 has left approximately 400,000 people without healthcare access, and aid workers have been forcibly evacuated from parts of Upper Nile state with 72 hours' notice – with government denial of access to opposition-held areas and systematic looting leaving the most vulnerable populations entirely unreachable. The already-underfunded humanitarian response would face collapse as needs outpace donor capacity, and the limited remaining health infrastructure – already severely degraded by looting and air strikes – would cease to function in the worst-affected areas.

updates.text: The risk has intensified after President Kiir dissolved the transitional government on 22 September, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December. The decree removed all five Vice Presidents, including the suspended First Vice President Riek Machar, dissolved the national and state legislatures, and replaced ministers and governors with caretaker appointees, ending the power-sharing arrangement set up under the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of Conflict in South Sudan. It followed amendments to the National Elections Act, signed on 21 September, that allow Kiir to remain in office with full powers throughout the election period. Kiir had also dismissed the chair of the National Elections Commission on 15 September without giving a reason. The South Sudan Opposition Movements Alliance has rejected the caretaker administration as illegitimate and the elections as a sham, and warned on 28 September that the crisis could lead to further violence and insecurity across the country. The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, which had already warned in August that elections without safeguards and inclusive dialogue could fuel renewed conflict and atrocity crimes, said the window to prevent a return to 2013–2018 levels of violence and displacement is closing. Government and Sudan People's Liberation Army-in-Opposition forces continue to fight in Jonglei and Upper Nile states, a conflict that predates the election, and no escalation directly linked to the election has been reported so far. Any such escalation during the election period would add to displacement in areas where humanitarian access is already constrained.

The Government's decision to press ahead with the December 2026 elections, sidelining the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan (R-ARCSS) in the process, has sharpened the risk of a return to full-scale civil war. On 22 July, President Kiir assented to a bill bypassing R-ARCSS consensus procedures. On 7 August, the Council of Ministers approved amendments stripping out the permanent constitution and national census as preconditions for the vote, over the objections of Machar's SPLM-IO faction. Machar himself remains under house arrest, facing trial without full due process guarantees, while a USD 75,000 party registration fee and the rejection of a rival "IO Party" registration have shut his faction out of the electoral process entirely, removing any incentive for the main opposition faction to accept the outcome peacefully. The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan has warned that these conditions, compounding the fighting and displacement already in progress, risk a rushed election, triggering renewed crimes.

Risk levels remained stable during May as no major clashes were reported, but humanitarian conditions continue to worsen. In the first three months of 2026 alone, 366,000 people lost access to MSF-supported healthcare following the bombing of Lankien and the looting of facilities across Jonglei. By the end of May, there was no surgical capacity remaining in the conflict-affected areas of the state. The Government committed on 8 May to facilitate humanitarian access to Akobo, though aid organisations warn access remains severely constrained. Akobo is projected to reach Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) food insecurity levels in April–July 2026, with over 7.8 million people nationally facing crisis-level hunger or worse. With the rainy season now underway, displaced families face growing isolation as flooding restricts humanitarian operations.

triggers.title: Cancellation of the December 2026 elections
triggers.description: With the 2018 peace process now dead, the December 2026 elections represented one of the few remaining frameworks for legitimate political transition — yet the prerequisites for a credible vote do not exist. The National Elections Commission remains unfunded, forces have not been unified, and active fighting makes campaigning impossible across large parts of the country. A further cancellation would likely be interpreted by opposition groups as a permanent consolidation of power by Kiir's government, deepening ethnic grievances and accelerating recruitment into armed factions
triggers.objective: Yes - 100% would be the election being formally cancelled leading to deepening conflict.

triggers.title: Economic collapse drives predatory violence by armed actors on both sides
triggers.description: Prolonged economic decline has left both sides severely weakened. Depleted state coffers and irregular pay have driven desertions and eroded morale, leaving government forces overstretched and increasingly reliant on proxy militias. With formal resourcing exhausted, offensives by government forces and militias have become as much about extracting taxes and looting civilian populations as achieving military objectives. Opposition forces face comparable pressures, with communal militias motivated more by the prospect of loot than political strategy. As both sides are compelled to prey on the communities they operate in, this dynamic risks transforming localised clashes into a self-sustaining cycle of violence, in which continued conflict becomes an economic necessity for armed actors, reducing incentives to negotiate and compounding an already acute humanitarian crisis.

triggers.title: Entanglement with the war in Sudan
triggers.description: South Sudan's conflict risks becoming entangled with the war in Sudan. Though Juba has maintained official neutrality, its close links to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which control much of Sudan's border with South Sudan, are widely observed. The Sudanese army is suspected of reactivating ties with Nuer opposition forces in a bid to pressure Kiir and disrupt RSF supply lines — a dynamic that, if confirmed, would effectively transform Upper Nile into a proxy theatre of Sudan's war. Compounding this, Uganda's continued military backing of Kiir is not guaranteed; Kampala's willingness to underwrite his survival is uncertain given South Sudan's economic collapse and Uganda's competing regional commitments. A withdrawal of Ugandan support, combined with increasing Sudanese entanglement, could significantly alter the military balance, accelerating conflict escalation and further collapsing humanitarian access

title: RSF expansion in Blue Nile state triggers displacement and protection risks
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
The RSF offensive launched in early 2026 against Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) positions in Baw county opened a new front in Blue Nile state. This has significantly increased the likelihood of conflict spreading to previously unaffected areas to the north, particularly Ed Damazine, the state capital, as well as the strategic corridor leading to the Roseires Dam. By advancing in Blue Nile state, RSF seeks to strengthen its position to recapture and control central Sudan, later opening a route through Sennar state.
Following heavy territorial losses in 2025, including entire states in central Sudan, RSF has reconstituted its operational capacity through its alliance with Abdelaziz Adam al Hilu's Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N/Al Hilu). Access to terrain under its control has provided RSF with defensive depth, cross-border supply lines, and logistical continuity. This enables it to sustain multifront operations and power its advance in Blue Nile, positioning the RSF for a prolonged and expanded offensive rather than a short-term tactical push and increasing the likelihood of escalation beyond the current front lines.
External facilitation further compounds these dynamics. SAF has repeatedly accused South Sudan and Ethiopia of enabling this mobilisation, with satellite imagery from February 2026 showing a logistics camp near the Ethiopian border in Benishangul Gumz despite official Ethiopian denial. If sustained, such external support would significantly raise the possibility of a scaled-up offensive by insulating RSF operations from battlefield setbacks
expectedImpact: If fighting expands north, large-scale displacement is likely towards Ed Damazine, other urban centres in northern Blue Nile, and neighbouring states. Newly displaced households would likely arrive with limited assets, increasing demand for emergency shelter, NFIs, safe water, sanitation, health services, and protection support. Overcrowding in informal settlements and host communities would heighten the risk of disease outbreaks, particularly where water and sanitation infrastructure is already weak. Fighting in populated areas, including drone strikes or shelling, could damage health, water, power, and road infrastructure, further reducing service availability and humanitarian access. Protection risks would likely increase, including family separation, GBV, child protection violations, psychosocial distress, and targeted violence against communities perceived as aligned with armed or political actors. Competition over land, livelihoods, and basic services could also trigger or worsen intercommunal tensions, particularly if displacement is framed as altering local power dynamics.
