updates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) expanded their territorial control in Blue Nile. On 11 August, the alliance captured Geisan, followed by Al Kurmuk on 13 August, after the Sudanese Armed Forces withdrew from the town. The offensive triggered significant displacement; more than 5,000 people had reached Ed Damazine by 18 August, while IOM reported nearly 14,000 displaced from Geisan and Al Kurmuk throughout the month. By 28 August, RSF and SPLM-N had claimed control of Bakori and Surkum military bases, while satellite analysis identified around 100 additional light technical vehicles at an Ethiopian base near Assosa, indicating preparations for further advances towards Ed Damazine.

The risk escalated in July 2026; conflict and displacement pressures in Blue Nile remained active, with Ed Damazine increasingly absorbing people displaced by months of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the alliance between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North (SPLM–N). On 23 July, a reported SAF drone strike hit a gathering of displaced people in Ed Damazine, killing several and underscoring the growing exposure of displaced populations in the state capital. In late July, community-based civil society responders warned of worsening humanitarian and health conditions among thousands of IDPs in Ed Damazine and surrounding areas, with heavy rains further aggravating conditions in camps and informal settlements. While there is still no clear evidence that the RSF/SPLM-N alliance has advanced decisively into Ed Damazine, the combination of continued clashes, displacement towards the city, drone incidents, and deteriorating camp conditions suggests the risk pathway is moving closer to materialisation.

title: RSF restoration of siege on Al Obeid, North Kordofan drives widescale displacement towards White Nile state
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Since October 2025, RSF has mobilised troops near Al Obeid's borders, including deploying combat vehicles along the western side. The sustained mobilisation and positioning of these forces indicate preparation for a renewed offensive to reinstate a siege of the city. A previous siege of the city between May 2023 and February 2025 demonstrated RSF's operational ability to isolate Al Obeid for prolonged periods, resulting in a significant deterioration in humanitarian conditions, including severe food insecurity.
RSF has a strong strategic incentive to restore the siege because of Al Obeid's role as a key logistic and commercial hub linking western and southern Sudan to Khartoum and central Sudan. Control of the city would provide RSF with greater leverage over supply routes, trade flows, and access to corridors into SAF-controlled areas, particularly central Sudan. Al Obeid's role as a major crop and livestock market and a gate for Kordofan exports further increases its strategic and economic importance to RSF.
Despite recent SAF advancements and repositioning in North Kordofan, fluid conflict dynamics and continued shifts in areas of control between SAF and RSF increase the likelihood of renewed attempts to siege the city over the next six months. This likelihood is further reinforced by increasing logistical and technical support provided to RSF by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which may improve the group's operational capacity to sustain offensive and siege tactics.
expectedImpact: A renewed RSF siege on Al Obeid could trigger large primary and secondary displacement, particularly among people already displaced from South and West Kordofan. Many households would likely move towards White Nile, especially Kosti, which remains linked by transport routes and has previously attracted people fleeing conflict in Kordofan. Movement restrictions, fear of ground assault, market disruption, and deteriorating living conditions would likely drive further departures. Inside Al Obeid, siege conditions would reduce access to food, fuel, medicines, markets, health services, and humanitarian assistance. Shortages and sharp price increases would weaken purchasing power and worsen food insecurity among residents, IDPs, and host communities. Because Al Obeid is a major agricultural and commercial market connecting Greater Darfur with eastern and northern Sudan, prolonged disruption could also affect wider trade flows and commodity availability across Kordofan and Darfur. Health impacts would include reduced medical supply delivery, strain on hospital capacity, and weaker outbreak response for cholera, dengue fever, and other diseases.

updates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) intensified around Al Obeid city, North Kordofan state. On 12 August, suspected RSF drones struck the city, killing two people and injuring others. From 14–15 August, RSF attacks on Um Arda locality, Tamid village, and Al Khor Al Abyad village, North Kordofan state, displaced 4,250 people; the attack on Um Arda alone killed 18 civilians and displaced more than 300 families towards Al Obeid. On 20 August, RSF attacks on Um Dareisa village and Al Shaqla village, North Kordofan state, killed six civilians and displaced more than 1,000 people towards Al Obeid city. These attacks increased pressure on the city and advanced the siege and displacement pathways of the risk.

The risk escalated in July as pressure from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on Al Obeid intensified into siege-like conditions, with repeated drone attacks, worsening shortages, and growing protection concerns. UN reporting describes Al Obeid as a key civilian, administrative, and humanitarian hub where RSF drone attacks and insecurity along exit routes have increased, while attacks have affected power stations, fuel depots, water facilities, transport routes, hospitals, markets, schools, and residential areas. Drone strikes have worsened water and fuel shortages in the city, while women and girls face the dual risk of daytime drone attacks and sexual violence when fetching water at night. Displacement pressure has also increased in Kordofan, with displacement sharply rising as the conflict escalated. Although widescale movement towards White Nile has not fully materialised, the siege and displacement pathway advanced significantly in July.

title: Interregional trade restrictions disrupt markets and deepen food insecurity in West Kordofan
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: The continuation or expansion of trade bans imposed in late 2025 by Khartoum, Northern, and North Kordofan states on the movement of goods into RSF-controlled areas would likely further restrict supplies to West Kordofan. These restrictions would affect food, fuel, medicines, agricultural inputs, and other essential commodities. West Kordofan is particularly exposed because it is landlocked and has historically depended on supply chains from northern and eastern Sudan, including routes through Khartoum, Red Sea ports, and Egypt. As formal routes become more restricted, markets are likely to rely increasingly on informal supply routes that are longer, more insecure, and more expensive because of checkpoints, unofficial taxation, transport delays, and insecurity. Alternative routes through Al Na'am market near Abyei provide some supply capacity but are limited and vulnerable to shocks, including fires, border tensions, and armed-party interference. If bans persist, supply shortages and price increases are likely to deepen food insecurity and market fragmentation across the state.
expectedImpact: Continued trade restrictions would reduce the availability of food, fuel, medicines, seeds, machinery, and other essential commodities in West Kordofan. Transport and transaction costs would likely increase and be passed on to consumers through higher prices, further reducing household purchasing power. Food insecurity would deepen as households face lower dietary diversity, reduced meal frequency, and less access to affordable staple foods. Limited agricultural inputs could undermine cultivation and reduce future harvests, while disrupted human and veterinary vaccination could increase disease risks and affect livestock productivity, livelihoods, and food availability. Rising food and fuel prices would likely also reduce access to health services, water trucking, transport, and humanitarian assistance. Households facing severe shortages may increasingly use harmful coping strategies, including consuming seeds reserved for planting, selling productive assets, and taking on debt. Deteriorating conditions could drive further displacement from rural and conflict-affected areas towards urban centres or assistance locations, increasing pressure on services and potentially worsening IPC Phase 5 risks in famine-risk localities.

updates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as restrictions on trade routes and markets increasingly constrained food availability and affordability in West Kordofan. On 6 August, Northern state authorities tightened controls on commercial trucks travelling towards Kordofan and Darfur, confiscating two trucks carrying food and fuel; millet reached SSP 900,000 per sack and onions SSP 2 million in An Nuhud locality, West Kordofan. By 15 August, households were consuming ambaz, an animal-feed byproduct, amid unaffordable food prices. On 26 August, authorities of the Rapid Support Forces closed public markets, restricted movement, and shut down Starlink services in An Nuhud, further disrupting commercial activity and food access. Although Khartoum state had reopened the export route on 14 August, continued restrictions elsewhere compounded market disruption.

The risk remained stable in July 2026, although there is limited reporting on new or expanded state-level bans on goods specifically affecting West Kordofan. The broader trigger pathway, however, remained concerning as conflict, access constraints, and rising costs continued to threaten food security and market functioning across the country. By mid-July, Sudan could slide further into hunger because of conflict, aid cuts, and rising agricultural costs, including higher diesel and fertiliser prices linked to wider regional disruption. Food insecurity continues to be reported, with Famine (IPC Phase 5) conditions under a worst-case scenario linked to intensified conflict and further restrictions on humanitarian access and the movement of goods and people. For West Kordofan, this means the risk has not clearly escalated through a new trade-ban development, but the underlying market and food security drivers remain highly fragile and could deteriorate quickly.

title: A rift between SAF and allied groups in Khartoum leads to worsening humanitarian conditions and protection concerns
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) face growing pressure from key external allies, including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the US, to distance itself from allied armed groups with political Islam leanings, including the Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade. This creates a risk of fragmentation within SAF's alliance structure, as attempts to contain, integrate, or undermine these groups could provoke resistance. SAF remains operationally dependent on allied armed groups for manpower, mobilisation, funding channels, and battlefield capacity across multiple fronts, making coercive integration difficult. Tensions have also emerged between SAF and factions linked to JEM, the Joint Forces, and other groups present in civilian and commercial areas in Khartoum. US designation and sanctions linked to the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood and Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade add further external pressure on SAF to disengage from these groups. If SAF pursues integration or restrictions while these actors retain military leverage and local positions, tensions could escalate into localised clashes, checkpoint competition, and fragmented territorial control in Khartoum and central Sudan.
expectedImpact: A rift between SAF and allied armed groups could trigger localised fighting around garrisons, military headquarters, markets, logistical infrastructure, and key transport corridors in Khartoum. Even if clashes remain localised, they could fragment areas of control and create parallel checkpoints, disrupting commercial goods, humanitarian assistance, fuel supplies, and population movement. Because Khartoum remains central to Sudan's trade and logistics networks, disruptions could affect food and fuel availability beyond the immediate conflict areas. Insecurity in densely populated urban areas would likely drive displacement eastwards or towards neighbouring countries, including Egypt, while discouraging returns. Protection risks would increase, including looting, arbitrary detention, ethnic targeting, abduction, sexual violence, and recruitment or forced conscription of young men and boys by competing factions. Humanitarian access would deteriorate as responders negotiate with multiple armed actors, increasing delays and operational risks. Damage or renewed insecurity around infrastructure and services would further strain health, WASH, shelter, and market systems.

updates.text: The risk remained stable during July 2026, with no clear public reporting of open clashes between SAF and its allied armed groups in Khartoum. The underlying drivers of the risk remained present. External pressure on SAF to distance itself from armed groups with political Islamist leanings continued in the background, following the earlier designation and sanctions targeting the Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade. The brigade continued to play an important role in SAF-aligned mobilisation, with links to Islamist networks and alleged ties to Iranian support, sustaining the potential for friction between SAF's military dependence on allied groups and external pressure to contain them. At the same time, developments in July centred more on drone strikes, the escalation in Kordofan, and RSF external support networks than on fragmentation among SAF-aligned groups in Khartoum. The risk therefore remains active but has not clearly moved closer to materialisation during July.

title: Long-range RSF drones targeting the eastern supply corridor and Port Sudan disrupt trade and aid delivery in Red Sea state
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: RSF tactics have increasingly shifted from ground offensives in SAF-controlled areas to long-range drone strikes. The May 2025 strikes on Port Sudan's fuel reservoirs demonstrated RSF's capacity to hit locations far from its main areas of control using long-range kamikaze drones. Port Sudan remains a strategic target because it continues to host key government, technical, and logistical functions, while the Port Sudan-Kassala-Gedaref corridor remains central to Sudan's economy and humanitarian response. Before the conflict, this corridor handled most international trade, and it continues to support imports, fuel supplies, and humanitarian cargo entering SAF-controlled areas. Targeting the corridor would allow RSF to undermine SAF supply chains and disrupt commercial and aid flows without needing to control territory in eastern Sudan. The likelihood of more frequent or damaging attacks would increase if RSF receives sustained external support, expands cross-border supply networks, or gains greater long-range drone capacity. Regional tensions around the Red Sea may further increase the corridor's strategic sensitivity.
expectedImpact: Repeated drone attacks on Port Sudan or the Port Sudan-Kassala-Gedaref corridor would likely disrupt trade and humanitarian supply flows into SAF-controlled areas. Damage to fuel depots, warehouses, port facilities, roads, or transport hubs could delay imports and onward dispatch, particularly if insecurity persists over several weeks. This would likely contribute to localised shortages and price increases for food, fuel, medicines, and other essential commodities, affecting urban populations, IDPs, and market-dependent households first. Fuel disruptions would have wider knock-on effects: humanitarian transport would slow, operational costs would rise, and the ability to move food, medical supplies, and relief items to field hubs would decline. Reduced fuel and power availability could also undermine WASH systems, water pumping, health facilities, cold chains, and disease response capacity. Although direct physical exposure may be concentrated around the corridor, the humanitarian consequences could extend across central and northern Sudan because of the corridor's central role in national supply chains.

updates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) resumed long-range drone attacks across areas held by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), increasing the threat to infrastructure supporting eastern supply routes. On 12 August, suspected RSF drones targeted Ad Damar, Al Obeid, Atbara, Bahri, and Um Durman; SAF air defences intercepted several drones, but others struck a mosque and an electricity transformer in Bahri and targets in Al Obeid, killing two people. On 18 August, SAF reported intercepting two RSF FH-95 drones near Jargeira and Bara, while further attacks were reported around Bara, Gebrat Al Sheikh, and the export route towards Al Obeid. The widening geographic reach and repeated attacks indicate an increased likelihood of disruption to transport and supply flows, although Port Sudan itself was not struck.

The risk remained stable in July, with no clear public reporting of renewed large-scale drone attacks on Port Sudan or sustained disruptions to the eastern supply corridor during the month. Concerns persisted that external supply networks could continue to provide the Rapid Support Forces with weapons, drones, and personnel, potentially sustaining or expanding its long-range strike capabilities. At the same time, the wider Red Sea environment became more sensitive during the month, with regional maritime security concerns increasing amid attacks and threats affecting shipping routes near the Red Sea and Suez-linked corridors.

title: RSF drone attacks damage the Merowe Dam and power grid in Northern state, disrupting health, food security, and public services
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Since 2025, RSF has expanded its long-range drone capabilities, including kamikaze munitions able to target infrastructure far inside SAF-controlled areas. Northern and River Nile states have already experienced repeated drone attacks on infrastructure, including strikes affecting Merowe Dam and associated power facilities. These attacks have mostly caused temporary disruptions rather than sustained structural damage, but they demonstrate intent and reach. The risk would increase if SAF-RSF fighting intensifies and RSF continues receiving external support that improves its long-range strike capacity. RSF has a clear strategic incentive to target Merowe Dam because it is Sudan's largest hydroelectric dam and supports electricity generation, irrigation, and economic activity across areas under SAF control. Disrupting the dam or the associated electricity grid would allow RSF to increase pressure on SAF governance, undermine public confidence, and disrupt services in areas away from front lines. While imminent large-scale escalation in Northern state is not clearly indicated, the dam's strategic importance makes damaging attacks a credible medium-term risk.
expectedImpact: Damage to Merowe Dam or associated grid infrastructure would likely cause widespread power outages across northern, central, and eastern Sudan, including Khartoum, Port Sudan, Ad Dabbah, Atbara, Dongola, and other dependent areas. Depending on repair capacity and the scale of damage, outages could persist for days or weeks. Health facilities would struggle to maintain surgeries, dialysis, oxygen services, vaccine preservation, and emergency care. WASH systems and water pumping would be disrupted, increasing waterborne disease risks, especially in overcrowded IDP sites and areas already facing poor sanitation. Power loss would also affect cold chains, communication, public services, and humanitarian operations. Irrigated agriculture linked to schemes such as Al Hamdab, Al Manasir, Amri, and Kihaila could be disrupted, reducing yields, household income, and food availability. Damage during cultivation periods would worsen livelihood losses and food insecurity, while repeated attacks could reduce confidence in relatively stable northern areas and undermine coping capacity over time.

updates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as damage to the Merowe power system caused widespread and prolonged electricity disruptions across areas under the control of the Sudanese Armed Forces. In early August, a fire at the Merowe Dam power station damaged transmission lines, leaving Khartoum, Northern, Red Sea, and River Nile states without stable electricity for nearly two weeks. Electricity was restored to Khartoum, Red Sea, and River Nile states on 16 August after repairs to damaged cables and a key transformer substation. Repeated drone attacks have also targeted Merowe infrastructure since the start of the conflict. Although the cause of the August fire was not established, the prolonged outage demonstrated the vulnerability of the Merowe-linked power system and its wider impact on essential services.

The risk escalated in July 2026 following renewed drone activity against power infrastructure in northern Sudan. On 16 July, drones from the Rapid Support Forces targeted a power station in the north, triggering a fire and injuring a security guard. The attack highlights the continued vulnerability of electricity infrastructure, as previous strikes on power facilities linked to the Merowe grid have caused widespread blackouts across Northern state, disrupting water pumping, health services, irrigation, and other essential public services. While there was no clear indication of structural damage to the Merowe Dam itself within the month, the renewed targeting of northern power infrastructure shows that the trigger pathway remains active.

title: Mass returns from eastern Chad exacerbate humanitarian needs in West Darfur State
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Deteriorating humanitarian conditions, aid shortfalls, and insecurity in eastern Chad are increasingly pushing Sudanese refugees to return to unsafe areas in Darfur, particularly West Darfur. Return movements rose in early 2026, with April arrivals into West Darfur nearly doubling compared with November 2025 levels. Many returnees cited access to resources, services, and humanitarian assistance as a main driver, suggesting that deteriorating conditions in displacement are influencing return decisions. Funding cuts and reduced assistance in Chad have weakened refugee coping capacity and strained already overstretched refugee-hosting areas. Planned relocations away from the Sudan border, following RSF cross-border attacks and Chadian military deployment, may increase uncertainty and pressure on some households to return prematurely. Political instability and tensions within Chad, including dynamics linked to alleged external support for RSF and tensions among groups affected by violence in Darfur, could make refugee-hosting areas less predictable. These factors may increase unsafe returns to Darfur despite continuing insecurity, limited services, and protection risks.
expectedImpact: Increased return movements from Chad would add pressure to West Darfur's already strained services, markets, shelters, and displacement sites. Returnees would likely require shelter, food, protection, health, WASH, and livelihood support, while host communities would face additional pressure on limited water, sanitation, health services, land, and markets. Overcrowding and poor WASH conditions would increase disease outbreak risks, particularly where vaccination and supplementation coverage are weak. Food insecurity would worsen as returnees and host households face high prices, limited income opportunities, and disrupted markets. Protection impacts would be significant: returnees may face movement restrictions, looting, intimidation, arbitrary detention, sexual violence, ethnically motivated attacks, and disputes over housing, land, and property. Non-Arab returnees may be particularly exposed when travelling through or returning to RSF-controlled areas. Damage to homes, roads, markets, and services would slow reintegration and could trigger secondary displacement if households cannot safely resettle or access livelihoods.

updates.text: The risk remained stable in July 2026, with continued pressure on Sudanese refugees and returnees in Chad, although there was no clear evidence of a sudden mass return movement into West Darfur during the month. By 30 June, more than 1.33 million people had crossed into Chad since the start of the Sudan crisis, including over 405,000 Chadian returnees, with further arrivals expected as conflict and food insecurity persist in Darfur. At the same time, severe funding shortfalls continued to reduce access to food, water, shelter, protection, and healthcare for refugees in Chad, weakening coping capacities in refugee-hosting areas.

triggers.description: Reduced food, health, shelter, or cash assistance would increase pressure on refugees to return despite insecurity.

triggers.title: Expansion of refugee relocation from border areas
triggers.description: Broader relocation away from the Sudan border or fear linked to military deployment could prompt premature return decisions.

title: Renewed violence in As Sweida or settler outpost establishment drives Israeli expansion in southern Syria, displacing civilians and restricting access
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
Since the fall of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024, Israel’s military presence in southern Syria has evolved from incursions into sustained territorial control. By early 2026, Israeli forces have expanded beyond the UN-monitored 1974 separation line into parts of Quneitra and western Dar’a, establishing military posts, outposts, and checkpoints. By mid-2026, the presence had become increasingly entrenched, with regular patrols and ground activity beyond the former separation area. Further expansion of positions, checkpoints, or closed military zones would indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. Sustained territorial control or restrictions on civilian access could increase local resistance and create conditions for further expansion towards areas linked to As Sweida.
Two pathways could accelerate or formalise this existing trajectory in the next three to six months. One is the revival of a proposal for a humanitarian corridor, first suggested in 2025 by Israeli officials to provide aid for Druze in As Sweida, particularly if renewed violence in As Sweida gives Israel a justification to intervene on behalf of the Druze and expand in southern Syria. The proposed corridor would connect the governorate with the Golan area, including Hader near Mount Hermon and Druze villages along the Syrian Golan. Although the proposal was previously rejected by the Syrian transitional Government, renewed violence or deterioration in As Sweida could bring it back into discussions and provide a pretext for expanding Israeli control or establishing protected access through southern Syria. While Israel framed its military intervention during the July 2025 violence as protecting the Druze, Druze opinion remains divided. One senior spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, has welcomed Israeli involvement, while the other two have consistently rejected foreign interference, and As Sweida's Druze security chief warned it had complicated reconciliation.
A second pathway is the activity of Israeli settlers seeking to establish a permanent presence. The Pioneers of Bashan,  an Israeli settler movement, have repeatedly attempted to cross into southern Syria and establish outposts, including around Hader and Mount Hermon, with their stated ambitions extending across As Sweida, Dar'a, and Quneitra governorates. More than 40 settlers entered the outskirts of Hader in April, while approximately 70–100 attempted to cross through Mount Hermon in July, followed by further attempts in August. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data indicates an upward trend in incursion attempts since April 2026, peaking sharply in July with six recorded events. Although the Israel Defense Forces have so far prevented permanent settlement, repeated attempts could increase pressure on Israeli authorities to eventually formalise such activity.
If either pathway materialises, further Israeli control and presence in southern Syria are likely to restrict civilian movement and access to agricultural land through additional checkpoints, patrols, and military restrictions. An expanded Israeli presence could also prompt resistance from Syrian government forces, as well as communities or armed groups in Quneitra and western Dar'a, increasing the probability of clashes around Israeli positions.
expectedImpact:
If the risk materialises, As Sweida, Dar’a, and Quneitra governorates are expected to face increased displacement, agricultural and livestock livelihood losses, deteriorating food access, and further disruption to water and essential services.
Further Israeli restrictions on farmland and grazing areas would reduce household income and food production. Between 70–80% of communities in southern Syria are dependent on farming for food, but Quneitra households in the immediate border zone have already reduced crop production because of Israeli military operations, further contributing to deteriorating food insecurity. In Dar’a, further restrictions on agricultural land could reduce household income during a critical period for potato and tomato production, with above-average 2026 harvests already generating limited returns because of weak prices and high input costs. Israeli incursions in July also cut agricultural labourers, herders, and farming households off from farmland and grazing areas during the harvest season, reducing cash income.
Expansion of Israeli positions or clashes around outposts and a protected corridor could trigger new displacement, particularly from communities surrounding Israeli positions. As Sweida is particularly exposed, with around 101,000 people internally displaced there by April 2026, equivalent to 21% of its population, while previous violence has displaced thousands towards Dar’a. Further displacement would increase pressure on host communities and already-strained services in Dar’a and As Sweida.
Further Israeli expansion could disrupt access to water infrastructure and sources in western Dar’a villages, particularly around new military positions or along a protected corridor. In Maariya, Israeli military activity around the site between May–June led to the sabotage of the village well, leaving residents dependent on costly private water supplies. In Abdin, piped water has been unavailable for a second consecutive year, with households paying around SYP 150,000 (USD 11.50) per tanker, while critically low water levels in Abdin Dam are already threatening irrigation in the Yarmuk Basin. Further Israeli expansion around these water sources could compound existing shortages, increase household water costs, and disrupt agricultural production.
Men in areas that may be affected by Israeli incursions could face increased protection risks from detention, interrogation, and movement restrictions. Israeli forces have continued to temporarily detain Syrian men during raids and at checkpoints, with some released after hours of questioning, while others have been transferred to Israeli detention facilities for months without publicly stated grounds. By 17 August, Israeli forces were still detaining at least 47 Syrians after the release of over 140 in July.

updates.text: The risk increased in September as Israeli ground activity in Quneitra and western Dar'a governorates intensified, while tensions in As Sweida persisted. During 1–7 September, 19 Israeli incursions were recorded in Quneitra (13) and Dar'a (6), including house searches, temporary checkpoints, and detentions. On 13 September, Israeli reservists called for deeper advances into southern Syria, while Israeli forces were already operating from 10 positions inside Syrian territory. On 22 September, Israeli forces shelled Jamlah and Abdeen villages in the Yarmouk Basin, followed by five incursions across Quneitra and western Dar'a within 24 hours on 29 September. In As Sweida, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri's factions continued calling for separation from Syria and blocked more than 13,000 students from reaching examination centres. Israel also called for the demilitarisation of Quneitra, Dar'a, and As Sweida, indicating continued efforts to shape the security environment in southern Syria.

triggers.title: Expansion of Israeli military control
triggers.description: A further expansion of Israeli positions, checkpoints or closed military zones beyond the current areas of control in Quneitra and western Dar'a could indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. If Israeli forces begin holding additional territory or restricting civilian access on a sustained basis, this could increase local resistance and create conditions for a broader Israeli-controlled zone extending towards areas linked to As-Sweida.

triggers.title: Renewed large-scale violence in As-Sweida
triggers.description: An escalation of violence between Druze groups, Syrian Government forces or other armed actors in As-Sweida could prompt Israel to reframe military intervention as necessary to protect the Druze population. This could revive calls for a Golan–As-Sweida humanitarian corridor and provide a justification for expanding or formalising Israeli military access in southern Syria.

triggers.title: Establishment of a settler outpost
triggers.description: Pioneers of Bashan or other Israeli settler groups successfully establishing a sustained civilian outpost inside southern Syria, rather than being detained and removed, could create pressure for Israeli forces to protect the settlement. This could accelerate the conversion of the existing military presence into a more permanent security or territorial arrangement.

title: Renewed cross-border strikes collapse the 2022 Houthi–Saudi truce, driving new displacement, disrupting imports, and reducing humanitarian access across Yemen
riskType: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale:
On 13 July 2026, the Iran-backed de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) announced the end of a de facto period of de-escalation with Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) of Yemen, increasing the risk of renewed cross-border and intra-Yemeni hostilities following a series of retaliatory actions. On the same day, the IRG said it had struck Sana'a International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing, while the DFA accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the attack. The DFA subsequently retaliated by launching missile and drone attacks against Abha International Airport, marking the first attack on Saudi territory since the 2022 truce. On 20 July, the DFA announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, describing it as a response to Saudi restrictions on DFA-controlled airports and seaports. The DFA has already targeted several vessels, including two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, in an attempt to enforce the blockade.
Fighting has also intensified between the DFA and the IRG along front lines in Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Ma’rib, and Ta’iz, predating but compounded by the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations. Saudi Arabia is the main IRG backer, and the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations has already prompted expanded military involvement. From 24–25 July, the Saudi-led coalition conducted strikes in Al Hodeidah, while the IRG air force struck DFA missile and drone launch sites and weapons facilities in Ma'rib and Al Jawf. These developments indicate that the escalation has expanded beyond isolated cross-border retaliation, increasing the risk of sustained intra-Yemeni conflict.
The first cross-border attack on Saudi Arabia since the truce is significant because it signals that both parties are becoming increasingly willing to use direct military force to pursue their objectives, weakening one of the key restraints that has sustained the de facto ceasefire. Both Saudi Arabia and the DFA have incentives to avoid a renewed large-scale conflict. Saudi Arabia seeks to protect its economic interests and avoid another costly war, while the DFA is unlikely to escalate unless it perceives increased Saudi military involvement or an opportunity to improve its strategic position. A miscalculation could trigger the renewal of conflict. Further attacks on Saudi territory or attempts to enforce a blockade of the Bab Al Mandab Strait would increase the likelihood of expanded or sustained Saudi and international military involvement in the Red Sea and Yemen. Saudi Arabia has already announced plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition on 30 July 2026.
Escalations between the DFA and Saudi Arabia would likely intensify fighting between the DFA and the Saudi-backed IRG, further restricting humanitarian access. Saudi air strikes on seaports and airports would disrupt commercial and humanitarian imports, triggering new displacement. Supply chain disruptions would increase commodity prices and erode purchasing power. Any disruption to shipping through the Bab Al Mandab Strait would also have cascading impacts on regional and global supply chains while aggravating needs in a country where over 22 million people require humanitarian assistance and 18.3 million are acutely food-insecure.
expectedImpact:
Renewed cross-border hostilities and intensified frontline fighting would likely increase civilian casualties, displacement, and humanitarian needs, particularly in Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Ma’rib, and Ta'iz. Escalating insecurity would further restrict humanitarian access, delay needs assessments, and disrupt the delivery of food, health, WASH, and protection assistance, especially in frontline communities and those with specific access constraints.
Saudi air strikes on transport infrastructure, seaports, and fuel supply routes, together with increased insecurity around the Bab Al Mandab Strait, would likely disrupt commercial imports and humanitarian supply chains. Higher shipping insurance premiums, transport costs, and fuel shortages would increase food and commodity prices, further reducing household purchasing power in a country heavily dependent on imports. Fuel shortages would also disrupt electricity generation, water pumping, health services, and the cold chain for medicines and vaccines, increasing the risk of disease outbreaks.
Escalation would likely trigger new displacement while exposing civilians to explosive ordnance and other protection risks. Households already experiencing severe food insecurity would have fewer coping options as livelihoods, markets, and humanitarian assistance are disrupted.
